From the London Times, July 30, 1850. Since the fortune of war and a sanguinary conflict were at last to terminate the dispute between the Crown of Denmark and the party which had sought to throw off the allegiance of the Duchies of Schleswig and Holstein, never was the just cause of authority more triumphantly defended, never did a people rally with more gallantry round their Sovereign and their standards, never were the intrigues of a foreign faction, which had fomented civil war in the dominions of a neighbouring and inoffensive State, more signally defeated ami punished. The battle of Idstedt, fought on the 25th of July between the Danish army commanded by its national chiefs, and the insurgent army fighting under the orders of its German officers, was accompanied by every circumstance which could enhance the glory of that hard-fought day to the Danish nation. The ranks of the enemy were swelled by volunteers from every part of Germany, arid led into action with all the experience of a well-known Prussian General and the impetuous bravery of the Bavarian Vox dek Taxn. The Danes stood alone in defence of their Sovereign and their country. Happily for that spirited people, no Russian or Swedish military auxiliary shared the honour of the victory. Their triumph and their thanksgivings are Unalloyed by the burden of an obligation even to those who wished them well. The moral support of Europe, which has faithfully attached itself to their cause, is all that they needed to enable themselves to vindicate their rights ;

and in defending the southern portion of their territories from invasion, they have shown that the dignity of a nation, the energy of a people, and even the brillani'y of its military exploits, are not measured by the space it covers on the surface of the globe. Although, therefore, this battle demonstrates the entire failure of the mediation which was intended to bring the dispute to a close by pacilic means, and although the treaty of peace just concluded in Berlin has had the immediate eiTect of staking the whole contest on the issue of one tiercely contested struggle, Denmark comes victorious out of this stern ordeal, and it is more than probable that if she had been relieved from the interference of other Powers she would long ago have terminated the whole quarrel. In one respect this occurrence is a repetition of the error committed in Italy after the first defeat of Ciiari.es Albert. If Radetzky had not been prevented from dictating a peace by an imperfect armistice imposed on him by other Powers after the retreat of the Sardinian army in August, 1848, the second campaign would not have been opened, and the battle o. Novara would not have been fought. So, likewise, il the Danes had not been prevented by ill-timid negotiations from following np their victory at Eredericia, the burdens of the intervening period and the frightful carnage of this last contest would have been spared. þÿ The only service rendered to Denmark by the negotiation lias been the withdrawal of the Prussian regi

incuts and the exclusion of Germany from this quarrel : that, indeed, was become inevitable, unless the allies of Denmark and guarantees of her territories were to have taken an active part in her support. The military operations of the day appear to have boon conducted by the Danes with equal skill and valour ; and although the field was most hotly contested on both sides by the stubborn valour of the troops, the defeat of the Holstein army seems to have been rendered inevitable by the inferior judgment of their German leaders þÿ the very men on whom they most relied. The position of the Holstein army in the south-eastern corner of the Duchy of Schleswig extended from Eckernforde and Schleswig on the coast to a small river called the Trccnc, flowing in a southerly direction, which bounded their extreme left. The Germans had shown no disposition to attempt the occupation of the disputed Duchy beyond these limits- But no sooner had the Danish commander-in-chief, General Vox Kroc.h, ascertained the fact of the renewed invasion of Schleswig by the insurgents, than he proceeded silently and steadily to execute the plan of a campaign which seems to have been prepared with consummate ability and performed witli equal precision and success. One Danish corps occupied the Isle of Fehmam, on the east coast of Holstein, to keep the attention of the enemy directed to that side, and possibly to effect a landing, in case of need, on the right flank of the Holstein army. The extreme right of the Danes advanced the whole lengtlj
of the Duchy without opposition. The main liody meantime took the high road midway between the two coasts of the isthmus. In Iladcrslebcn, Apen-

3 þÿ 1. A 7 1 3. radc, and Flensbnrg, the Danish colours wero hailed with enthusiasm ; and from the latter town the line of march deviated to the southwest, on the road to Husuin, until it arrived on the left bank of the Treene, on a level with the Holstein left wing under General Vox deu Taxn. Two severe skirmishes ensued in an attempt to force the passage of the river, but in the mean lime the bulk of the Danish army was concentrated somewhat more to the north ; a feigned attack was made on the Holstein right, General Von dek Tann with his light horse on the extreme left was cut off lrom the main body, and the Danish infantry with a powerful park of artillery bore dow n with irresistible gallantry on the centre of the enemy under General Wielisen himself; the battle was then fought for many hours with extreme tenacity on the direct road t<j the town of Schleswig. The Germans were at length driven back with great loss, and although they assert that they retreated in good order, the Danes unquestionably entered Schleswig that same night, whilst the enemy withdrew even from Eckernforde. þÿ The northern Duchy was thus at once cleared from the invading force, and it remained doubtful whether the Danish General would not pursue his advantage by the occupation of Holstein. At any rate we may assume that all military resistance on the part of tiie Duchies is at an end. Kiel and Rendsburg must at least be held by the þÿKing troops, s and the Provisional Government is probably dissolved. We earnestly

hope that uo mistaken views of pacification will now be put forward to prevent the real practical settlement of the question. It is a misfortune, and in every respect a disgtace, that this terrible Waste of human life should have been required to dispel the delusions of the German demagogues, and to atone for the want of resolution and plain dealing on the part of the great Powers of Eurojie. But since the battle has been fought and won, let Denmark and the world at least have the fruits of it ; and let us hear no more of a cause which had been abandoned by those who once professed to defend it. It is hard to lay aside a cherished illusion and to witness the destruction of a policy which had influenced the imagination of an enthusiastic people, hut this decisive event must bring home the conviction to every professor utriusque juris throughout Germany, that the rights of an independent, though a small, nation arc not to be disposed of by academic casuistry or by popular songs. It the Germans are bent on regarding this termination of the contest as a defeat to themselves, we must say such a humiliation is entirely self-imposed. No one in Europe, and especially no one in this country, has shown any disposition to impinge on tllcir rights, to contest their lawful authority, or to reduce their just influence ; but when any State or any people thinks that it can remove the landmarks ol Enrol a»d dictate single-handed to its | neighbours, the common sense of justice and the com- !

moil interest of peace resist 6uch aggressions. If Germany had really determined, as some of her indiscreet champions ventured to assert, to fling her legions into this contest, she would have incurred the calami- j tics and the guilt of a general war, and of war without an ally. She more wisely stood aloof, and repressed I a sympathy she did not affect to conceal. The result proves that it is not by the native force of the þÿDuchies but by the improper interference of Germany, that the j contest has alone been protracted to this day, and all the evils those provinces have endured rest upon the | bead of the reckless agitators who succeeded in misleading public opinion in Germany on this question. þÿ On the part of Denmark, the efforts and the sufferings of a gallant nation have been gloriously rewarded, and though the time is now come when the rights of the Crown may be enforced without further contestation, we hope that they will be accompanied with institutions calculated not only to preserve the union of the Danish monarchy, but to secure the liberties and the affections of a free and not undeserving people. w u<s- . þÿ

Remark on Constitution A Lmx by Sir Richard Phillips. þÿ Law, in its general sense, signifies a rule of social conduct, which superior authority has dictated, and which the community are bound to obey. The law of nature is a principle of self-love, or the individual pursuit of happiness. The law, in practice, however is the primary and chief cause of half the miseries of human þÿlife.

þÿ Government, a subject deeply interwoven with the happiness and comforts of the human race, has been that arrangement over which wisdom has always had the least control. Most governments are founded on usurped power, and tire results of pride and sellinterest. For the most part, they have arisen front military conquest, or some accidental ascendancy during tin insurrectionary movement ; and the rule of government has, in consequence, been the will of a leader on one side, and abject submission þÿol the rest of the community on the other. No check on power has existed but in the forbearance or idleness of the ruler, or in the scruples ol his agents; and, if checks have been introduced, they have been either mere concessions of policy, or have been rendered inefficient by colorable forms, or by various sinister and counteracting inþÿfluences. þÿ The courts of justice are open to all, but they must ho entered with plenty of þÿmoney. þÿ The law of primogeniture is the great curse of British society. It enables property to accumulate by heirship faster than tv industry; it generates a race of spoiled children of fortune, and simultaneous races of proud þÿbeggars. þÿ None hut vain sovereigns add to the splendor of palaces, before cottages are made comfortable. These ought to be regarded as the porticoes of þÿpalaces.

It has also been said that 1 made 150 lllids: Sugar this year, which is wrong. 1 clearly stated that I had made that quantity of Sugar last year which was the crop of 1810, þÿ 100 llhds; of which was made from 5 pieces of Plants, it must naturally follow that those 5 pieces wore established in 1818. This year 1 had only 2 pieces in plants for want of labour to open the land, for next year 1 have 7 pieces in plants, al| done with the plough. I.V ItOPEAN TIMES. Liverpool, August 17. DOllAltK Sc TI1E DUCHIES. Hamburgh, July 30. þÿ The Danish report of the battle of Idstedt is published. It reports 12 officers killed, and 78 wounded ; 104 non-commissioned officers and privates killed, and 2300 wounded ; 1000 prisoners were taken, and two pieces of cannon recovered and five captured from the enemy. 2000 wounded insurgents are stated to be in Schleswig Holstein. The Danish army is perfectly ready for fresh operations. General Willisen has also published his report of the battle. lie is not able yet to give an accurate return of the killed and wounded, or the total loss, but regrets the large number of officers killed and wounded. As soon as their loss shall be replaced, the army would be as ready for action as at the first. þÿ The loss of men would be supplied from the reserve. He is well supplied with provisions, and bad taken but few prisoners. Mr. Nouensen, British consul and agent to þÿLloyd s, at Eckernford, was arrested on the 2nd by the commander of the Schleswig-Holstein gun-boats, and directly afterwards conveyed on board the steamer Reil, lying there, which immediately left for Sonning, whence the consul will probably be conveyed to Kiel or Rendsburg. He reserved to himself his legal rights to the utmost extent, because he was compelled to yield to force. A telegraphic despatch from the Cologne Gazette, dated Hamburgh, 7th instant, states that General Willisen has declared that he will hold the Danish provinces responsible for

whatever may happen to those of the Schleswig-Holstein party. No change had taken place in the position of the armies. General Willisen had issued another proclamation, praising his troops and declaring that they cannot be driven from the soil of Schleswig except by a second and third battle, and they will be bloodier than the first. The Danish force is estimated at 42,000 to 44,000 men. The ardour for the Holstein cause is abating at and near Hamburgh. By transit steamer from Hamburgh we have the following: þÿ From the Hamburgh Borseniialle, of the Oth instant þÿ 4i.to.na, August 5. A collision be- þÿ tween the two advanced guards of the Danish and Holstein armies is said to have taken place on Friday, near Wohlde, which is reported as follows : þÿ 150 men of the 1st Jiegcr corps were behind an entrenchment with four guns, and from 600 to 700 Danes, with two guns and a number of waggons, were seen along the streets. The Danes were allowed to approach within half gun shot, when they fired into them with grape, followed up by two volleys from the J.cgers ; the Danes retreated, taking their wounded. Kiel, August 5 þÿ of the Danish army is said to have been encamped near Hollingstadt, and corps will probably proceed in a new direction towards Eckernford.

s tr» <8 s< a a a'? as. The protocol relating to the affairs of Holstein and. Denmark was definitively signed at the Foreign Office on the evening of the 2nd inst. The document was signed by the representatives of Denmark, France, Great Britain, Russia, Sweden, and Norway. The representative of Austria was present, but expressed a wish to consult the cabinet of Vienna, and the protocol was consequently left open for the court of Austria. The Prussian representative was not present, and the Prussian Government is understood to have protested ; but the protocol was nevertheless left open for the court of Prussia. The principal articles of this declaration were already known. They express the unanimous desire of the powers for the maintenance of the Danish possessions in all their integrity, and the wisdom ol the King of Denmark in regulating the succession in his royal house. It is to be hoped that the production of the agreement will put an immediate end to an unjust and unnatural war. The Austrian cabinet has recommended the Danes not to cross the Eider, and the latter have determined to obey the recommendation. By accounts from the head-quarters at Rendsburg we learn that an explosion of the laboratory of the artillery had taken place. Ninety-one persons killed by the explosion have been buried ; thirty-live wounded, some severely, and eleven put down as missing. Many bodies are so mangled that they cannot be identified. Twenty-two cadets oftlie artillery school are among the killed. Scarcely a house

in the town has entirely escaped from the concussion. The effect of the catastrophe on the public mind had been very depressing. The Northern Free Press, of Hamburgh, has the following from Rendsburg of the 8th : þÿ Since eight þÿo clock this morning fighting has been going on in our centre. The Danes attacked us with large forces near Sorgbruk. We heard the cannon for hours, but it gradually became more distant, and for the last two hours we have heard nothing. It is said that the Danes have been driven back towards Kropp, and that we have made some prisoners ; but it is probable that it is only a rcconnoisance, and that the battle will take place toþÿmorrow. The following from Hamburgh of the Oth appears in the Brussels journals : þÿ þÿ We have this moment learned that of the Danish army yesterday attacked that of Holstein on all the line ; the attack was principally made on the right and left wings ; the centre was only feebly assailed. It is possible that the Danish general desired to take advantage of the tumult occasioned at Rendsburg by the explosion of the shell manufactory to make the attack. The result has been the abandonment by the first The main strength ! corps of light infantry of Holstein of the town of Fredcrichstadt, situated in Schleswig, and its retreat on this side of the Eider. At about five þÿo clock a sharp cannonade was heard between the shore, if not from our very arsenals and

centres of the two armies, both in the Schleswig territory. If a second battle should take place, the result will probably be known þÿto-morrow. Accounts from Hamburgh, oftlie 10th, state that some severe skirmishing took place the day before, which ended in the Danes taking possession of Frederichstadt : this had evidently been the object of the movement. The Danish Ministers of Finance and Justice, accompanied by Russian and French Envoys, who will be speedily joined by an English Envoy, have arrived at Raiding, to negotiate a settlement of differences between the belligerents, and a cessation of hostilities has, it is said, taken place. >>««« New Yoik Herald. The Release of the Con toy Prisoners. þÿ We have received private information from the highest authority in Havana, which throws additional light upon the release of the Contoy prisoners, and upon the future designs relative to the prisoners taken in the Georgian and Susan Loud. When the steamer Vixen arrived at Havana, Commodore Morris, who was commissioned by the United States government to demand the release of those incarcerated in the dungeons of the Moro, called on the Captain General. The Captain General fixed, as a time for an interview, twelve, þÿo clockof the same day. It appears, however, that at eleven þÿo clock, one hour before the time specified, forty-two of the prisoners were released, each being informed that, if lie should ev er be taken within the dominion of Cuba or Porto Rico, he would be liable to im-

prisonment for two years ; and it was added, as a melancholy consolation, that a chain and ball would be attached to bis ankle, to control any indisposition toward any active labor imposed by the authorities. With respect to the other prisoners, matters may not turn out quite so favorably. The forty-two who have been released wrere tried, and the evidence was found insufficient to produce conviction, even though one of their own number turned þÿState s evidence. The remaining prisoners it appears, are held by a stronger claim than that which detained the others. They were connected with vessels in which were large munitions of war, and the sailing papers of which made no mention of these formidable agents of invasion and revolution. Not being able to explain to the satisfaction of the Cuban authorities, their position in this particular, they are liable, under the law of nations, to suffer the penalty which their situation has brought upon them. In view of their probable lamentable end, we cannot refrain from referring once more to the conduct, or rather w ant of sagacity and activity, display ed by the recent government at Washington. Here were arms, ammunition, means, and appliances of war, proceeding in American vessels directly from our

depositories, without a single obstacle appearing in the shape of government power to avert the certain result predicted by every sensible man in this country. While we can hope that those now in the hands of the Cuban authorities may be released, because they are the dupes of men far more guilty, yet what shall we say of that cabinet, whose supercilious indifference, or rather negative assistance, has done so much to jeopardize the liberties and lives of an indiscreet portion of our citizens? They have much to answer for in this business ; and our only hope is that the present government at Washington will be able to lessen the aggravation of their þÿpredecessor s sins, by diminishing the terrors which may result, if some judicious action does not mark our future correspondence with Cuba respecting this unhappy affair. While we would have the þÿlaw of s nations respected, we would see Spain take a nobler step than to punish the weak victims of indiscretion now in her power, for the want of the true culprits who are roaming through this land in search of some new nucleus of mischief.

Tiie Deaths of Great Men. It may be some consolation to the little to know that their lives are as safe as those of the great, and that on the bed of sickn ss there is, perhaps,

more probability that the humble attendance they may have, will often be more successful than the crowd of doctors who are called to the bedside of the great. As a case in point, suppose a poor man had fallen down and broken Ins rib. lie would not have been carried into an elegant drawing room ; he would not have been placed upon a patent hydraulic bed ; he would not have had all the talent of the land surrounding him ; but his ribs would have been examined, the fracture would have been discovered, and, it may be, his life saved. Not so with Sir Robert Peel : they spared his feelings, and forbore to examine and find out where he was hurt, so that he literally died under their hands, without receiving any aid from them, in reposed to kick out of the way. We spect to the real cause of Ins death, and without their even knowing where | he was hurt ; for they never found out that a rib was broken till after his death. Strange comment this upon our confidence in the great names and snow, which the children laugh at and a great host of surgeons and doctors. pelt till it is knocked over and lost, Had it been a poor man in New York, and he could not hear to be touched

have given him a dose of chloroform, set the fracture at once, very probably have sent him hack to his work in a fortnight. There are many similar cases among the great, perhaps that of General Tay lor may he accounted one. These cases are so numerous, that it would seem almost better for the ricli to wish to he poor as it certainly is better for the poor to he contented, and not to wish to be rich.

IT having come to tny knowledge that a wrong construction has been put on my last communication to the Agricultural Society respecting Tmplemcntal Cultivation, I beg leave to state that I merely pointed out the absolute necessity of generally adopting the system as the only means of keeping up the Cultivation, "not as a cheaper mode of Culture," but the only resource we have, left to us. It has also been said that I made 150 1 1 lids: Sugar this year, which is wrong. 1 clearly stated lhat I had made that quantity of Sugar last year which was the crop of 1841), þÿ 100 llluls: of which was made from 5 pieces of Plants, it must naturally follow that those 5 pieces were established in 1818. This year 1 had only 2 pieces in plants for want of labour to open the land, for next year 1 have 7 pieces in plants, all done with the plough. I will give a statement of the expense attending the new system at the next meeting. It is evident that the Manual Labour is not more than half sufficient to keep the Island in Cultivation, 1 therefore declare that unless other and more efficient means are used, than depending on the manual labour now at command, the Island must be ruined. And again that I have proved the Implcmental Cultivation, to he far superior to the Old System, and invite all persons to come and see the Canes produced, and the implements in opera- tion see and believe," no theory, " such is the advantage of the wide flat bank, that those who adopt it imme-
diately will do well.

We publish elsewhere an authentic copy of the protocols finally agreed upon and executed on Friday last at the Foreign-office by the Plenipotentiaries of the chief Powers of Europe. The principal articles of this declaration were already imperfectly known to the public by the versions of the former protocol given in the German journals ; but as some doubt has been thrown ori the intentions of the great Powers, on the language of this document, and on its application to the present state ol affairs in Germany and the Duchies, we hope that the production of the agreement itself, as definitively executed by all the foreign Ministers concerned, and in the presence of the Charge d'Aflaires af Austria, will promote its object, and hasten the cessation of an unjust and unnatural war. No time should, therefore, be lost in bringing this distinct announcement of the principles recognised by the Conference to the knowledge of those Mho commenced this insurrection, and are still instigating these hostilities. We have no doubt that the German Governments are, one and all of them, heartily sick of the very name of 8chlcs wig-Hoi stein, and that although some of them may have the baseness to regard this contest as a safety-valve to relieve the revolutionary pressure on themselves at the expense of an unoffending neighbour and confederate, the wisest statesmen of Germany have long since discovered that this struggle serves to keep alive nil those had passions of

the late general convulsion, which have done the rulers and the nation incalculable injury. It cannot, therefore, be supposed that the Governments represented. by the Conference of London are really at variance with the Governments of Germany on this question, or that Prussia hcrscli can have the fatuity to adhere to a course entirely isolated from the common policy of the rest of Europe. The false steps heretofore taken in her name prove, no doubt, very embarrassing to her now ; but it is not unfair

that she should expiate an outrage by an inconsistency, and the Cabinet of Berlin probably rejoices at this very moment that the other Powers of Europe are taking a course calculated to accomplish that which she herself is least able to attempt or to avow. The contention, then, lies not between the German States and the rest of Europe, but between the misguided and excited public opinion of Germany, which has been decoyed into its present humiliations by a strange mixture of enthusiasm and intrigue, and the public law and policy of Europe as laid down with authority by a free conference of the great Powers. The question is, which of these forces is to decide this controversy, and to govern the world. þÿ If the popular passions of the Germanic race are to give the law, they are leadins to a war as destructive in its effects as it has been ridiculous in its causes þÿ a war of which Germany herself would be the theatre, and the victim. For half a century Europe had accustomed itself to look upon the warlike passions of the French democracy as the greatest peril to the general peace. Perhaps we did injustice to the thrift and disposition of France; for certain it is that the Government sprang from universal suffrage has shown no disposition to attack other countries, and tiic agitators who speculated on war as a means of revolution have failed to gain a hearing. But that class of nefarious agitators has unhappily turned with more effect to Germany. There they have succeeded in deluding

a large portion of t he people into a belief that their honour and interests as a nation are mixed up with this Danish contest, and if the question were now to be decided by popular assemblies or German democratic bodies, it would be blown at all hazards into a perfect conflagration. They have yet to learn that a popular war cry is as foolish as it is odious, until that solemn day comes when the violation of some positive right, 1 lie aggression of a foreign Power, or some stain upon the public honour which nothing else can efface, calls an entire nation, reluctant but unanimous, to the field. It is superfluous to add that it becomes the duty of the German Governments, and of the rest of Europe, temperately but firmly to resist these the companionship of Joubert, has, dangerous passions and illusions, which, indeed, can scarcely be said to belong to the true nature or character of the German people, although they have been profusely strewn among them by the destructive bands which have lately passed over that country. Morally speaking, the Conference of London now stands pledged to maintain the ground of legal rights and the cause of peace against this aggressive spirit- Practically, that object can only be secured by causing the insurgent army in Schleswig-llolstein, now hourly recruited by German adherents, and supplied by German contributions, to disperse and lay down its arms. We give the Conference full credit for having accomplished the first of these objects by its

&T U 'A & 2 S ATI 3. declaration ; but that object tells for comparatively little in flagrant war, and the repetition of such sanguinary battles as that of Idstedt will be now more than ever an opprobrium Europe. to If the Ilolsteiners and Germans are fighting j a o for the acquisition of Schleswig, they are fighting for that which they are now distinctly told they never shall have; for though we trust that Denmark will still scorn to owe to foreign aid what she can do alone, there can now be no doubt that a momentary success by the opposite party would only bring about a more total defeat of their cause by such forces as the case might require. þÿ If the llolsteiners are fighting for the rights of their own duchy, that is a subject perfectly open to discussion and amicable arrangement.. Of reasonable causes of war they have literally none, and they are playing at a game at which it is impossible for them to win the stakes, while they are throwing away the rights on which they might rely in negotiation by risking them in the field. For instance, Schleswig is already of. facto and dF jure conquered, and if there were any arguments for her independence before they are now disposed of by the battle of Idstedt. One more such defeat and the fate of Holstein will be entirely in the hands of the Court of Copenhagen; and while the Stadtholderatc speculates on drawing Germany on to interfere in its behalf, it is in reality drawing the rest of Europe on to resist its pretentions. These considerations

are decisive as to the expediency of making peace, even in the interests of had left her home lie had but two interthe Duchies, if policy and public duty are to decide that question. The guilt of prolonging the war rests, in the first instance, on its authors who have still the power of terminating its horrors ; but if they persist in their reckless course, it would become the duty of all the parties to the protocol of London to consider and to adopt the most direct and effectual means of putting an end to such a contest.

On Saturday last, wrought up to frenzy by the disgrace which he had entailed upon her, she undertook, with the aid of relatives and friends, to wreak a summary revenge. She visited Joubert at his store, corner of Julia and Tuhoupitoulas-streets, and invited him to walk with her, stating the time that at she had escaped from the custody of her family. The father of Joubert, suspecting danger, insisted that he should not leave the house ; but the fellow declared that he would face the world if Rebecca were with him, donned his best attire, and accompanied her. They proceeded to the corner of Annunciation and Race-streets, followed at a short

distance by three of her friends, who were there to aid her in case of an emergency. During the walk, Joubert communicated the fact that he had offered 1000 to an acquaintance, if lie would assist him in again taking her from the guardianship of her family. While thus conversing Rebecca suddenly threw off her bonnet, upbraided him in violent terms for his infamous course, told him that she was satisfied of the falsehood of his solemn oath that lie was not of a negro blood, nor a married man, and then, with a motion too quick to allow his retreat, she drew a pistol from her breast, presented it, and fired, the ball penetrating his check and shattering the teeth of his left jaw. Joubert staggered, o © but the desperate girl finding her work but partially done, instantly drew another pistol, and, planting it directly in his face, pulled the trigger. The weapon failed to second her intention. It snapped, and her friends fearing violence from Joubert, immediately came up to her aid. One of them, pistol in hand, advanced to the wounded man and offered a fair combat ; but Rebecca, declaring that she would vindicate her own cause, snatched the third weapon and again essayed to shoot the late companion of her fight. Joubert retreated as the infuriated girl advanced, and he owes his life to the fact that she could not, with her ignorance of the weapon, discharge the load. A parley here ensued in this singular affair, and Joubert, before the crowd of persons assembled, declared that after Rebecca

views with her, both in the presence of others. lie expressed himself most penitent for his intended crime and past deceptions, and avowed that he had received but his deserts. These statements appearing satisfactory to the parties, they drove off in a carriage, leaving Joubert to seek relief for his wound. þÿ One of the police came upon the spot at the close of the affair, and attempted to arrest the girl, but we understand that Joubert said that lie had no charge to make, and had merited all that he had received, upon which no further effort was made to detain her. þÿ New Orleans Bee, July 10.

Punishment in Morocco. þÿ A Mogador letter of the 30th ult., relates a fact þÿ which occurred on that day, and which gives an idea of the manner in which offenders are punished in Morocco : þÿ " A Moor struck another with a stick with such violence, that he left him half dead on the spot. For this he himself was basted at the usual rate of 100 strokes for each struck by the assailant, and afterwards sent to prison. Unfortunately for him, the other man died within half an hour; which having come to the knowledge of the authorities, the prisoner was brought out, flogged about the streets, until, no longer able to stand, lie fell down, and was then dragged through the city. A Santon (Moorish recluse), however, took him under his protection, and got him conveyed to a
mosque. But it was too late ; he breathed his last, and three hours after both murderer and victim were buried at the same time."

A Female Aeronaut. þÿ Mrs. Graham, with three of her daughters and her son, ascended from Baysvvater, on Monday week, in a new balloon, called the Victoria and Albert . The party descended safely in Richmond-park. Mrs. Graham has written as follows to one of the papers : þÿ " I cannot omit noticing the extraordinary admiration of my daughter Alice, who accompanied me on Friday night from Vauxhall Gardens, at the astonishing view of London, at midnight, being the first and only attempt made by females to conduct the management of a balloon at night, and so much pleased am I with the nerve exhibited by those of my daughters w ho have hitherto accompanied me (four in number), that if, on trial, I find the others of equal spirit, which I doubt not, I feel disposed (God willing) to ascend with my seven daughters at the great national exhibition of 1851."

vrsi AL PHENOMENA. 'Flie blind make up for defect of sight by the accuracy and sensibility of their touch, and by habits of association between the touch, memory, and judgment. Stanley, the organist, and many hhnd musicians, have been the best performers of their time ; and the blind discriminate sounds at a distance with infinitely greater precision than persons who depend on their visual organs. Miss Chambers, a schoolmistress at Nottingham, could discern that two boys were playing in a distant part of the room, instead of studying their hooks, though a person who saw them, and made no use of his ears, could not perceive that they made the smallest noise ; and in this way she kept a most orderly school. So Professor Sanderson could, in a few moments, tell how many persons were in a mixed company, and presently discriminate their sexes by the mere rustling of their clothes. Stanley, and other blind persons, played at cards by delicately pricking tliern with a pin. A French

3 T ATU lady could dance in figure-dances, sew tambour, and thread her needle. The ear, too, guides as to distance, by reflection of sound, and within these few years a blind man, from his infancy, was a surveyor and planner of roads in Derbyshire. When a sense is wanted, the others are cultivated with care. Home blind persons say they can discriminate colours : others deny the power. Miss Mc'Evoy, of Liverpool, could read, says Dr. lienwick, by laying glass over a book, and distinguish objects in the street, by feeling on tiie glass of the window. The late blind Justice Fielding walked in my room, for the first time, when he once visited me, and, after speaking a few words, said, k' This room is about 22 feet long, 18 wide, and 12 high j" all which ho guessed with accuracy by the ear. þÿ Dak win.

LITERATURE. Colonists are grossly abused by the exporters of books, and the ignorance of merchants ; and they get few books but such as are mere waste paper in England. The merchant usually orders a case ot books, of 100/. or 500/. value, forgetting that there are books of every variety of intrinsic worth ; and then the dealer avails himscli of this inadvertency, and fills the case or cases with none but such books as few ever saw in England, and which can generally be bought at the price of waste paper. Fine binding is the chief feature of books thus sent abroad. The literary education of women began to prevail in the early part of the 17th century. Till then, few were taught more than to read, but writing was then superadded with music, dancing, and French. In 1020, neither of Shakspeare's daughters could write. The change o wrought o changes o in literature. To provide books for female readers, novels were contrived ; and, owing to women having leisure, they were multiplied ; and, since 1780, have so grown in number, and commercial importance, as almost to supercede all other books, and render them but secondary, in profit, to authors or publishers. þÿ Phillip's Million of Fuels.

MANUFACTURES. It is a rule with the Chinese, which has tended to perpetuate their empire, that nothing shall be made by the direction of natural powers which can be made by hand. Hence, family employments are constant from age to age ; but, with us, every kind of competition is encouraged, and no man can anticipate for his children. Society, in consequence, is a ruinous scramble. No manufacture ought to be tolerated which docs not pay the operatives

the wages of subsistence ; and, which affords no profits to merchant manufacturers beyond the exactions and cribbings from the dependent operatives. Hindoo manufactures are generally imitated in Europe, and even retain their names. Calicoes, cossacs, jaconets, boucks, chintzes, mulls, japans, ballusores, bandannas, pulleates, ginghams, &c. &c. are all Indian n i tries, and mere imitations. The Hindoos seem to be in manufactures like the Greeks in architecture, even in the minute circumstances of package, salvage, fringe, &c. þÿ Ibid. The building of iron ships is extensively progressing on the river Tyne. Gums for the dcerepid mouth are now being manufactured from gutta percha. From the San Fernando Gazette, Trinidad, August 31, 1850. THE ACTING WARDEN of the South Naparima Western Ward requests the Editor ol the San Fernando Gazette will give publicity to the Circular sent herewith : þÿ (CIRCULAR.) GOVERNMENT HOUSE, 28th August, 1850. The French Government having determined upon granting Compensation to the owners of those Slaves who fled from time to time from the island of Martinique and Guadeloupe, and took refuge in the British West India Colonies; and having deputed as their Agent, M. JOUBERT, for the purpose ot visiting the British Colonies, in order to ascertain the existence of any

of these people ; the Governor is anxious to afford this gentleman every facility in his mission. With tins view, therefore, I am directed by His Excellency to request that you will cause enquiry to he made, whether there are any parties residing within your Ward, who were originally slaves in either of the above mentioned Islands and if so, that you will transmit to me a return of their names, and the dates of their arrival in this Colony, with their places of abode. In making your enquiries, you will he cautious not to give any alarm to these people, hut explain to them, that all that is intended by the enquiry is simply to ascertain their existence, so that their late owners may receive the amount of Compensation which has been awarded by the French Government. As Mr. JOUBERT'S stay in this Colony is limited, it is desirable that you should immediately proceed to make your enquiries, and transmit to me the returns called for on or before the 9th proximo. I am, Sir, Your obedient humble servant, THOMAS F. JOHNSTON, Col. Secretary. The Warden South Naparima Western Ward.

He spoke of his impending fate with fortitude and calmness, and appeared perfectly resigned. He was pleased, and felt graleful that the time of his execution had been kept from the knowledge of his family. At dawn of day various noises appeared to disturb him, and he became agitated, but would soon regain his confidence. By the advice of Physicians he breakfasted on tea and coffee wiih bread. He made all preparations to ascend the scaffold with firmness, and did so. About 300persons were admitte d within the jail yard. The house tops in the vicinity of the jail were crowded with persons among whom were many women. The streets leading to the jail were also thronged. At nine o'clock, after performing religious services in his cell, the prisoner was brought out attended by his spiritual advisers, the sheriff, jailor, <Mc. He walked erect, and ascended the scaflbld with a firm step. Here he remained shaking hands and engaged at times in meditation. At twenty minutes before 10 o'clock the cap was drawn over his face. He bade adieu to the sheriff, jailor, and others, and soon after the trap fell, launching his spirit into eternity. He seemed to die with but few struggles. After death his body was taken back to the cell, and there it will remain until dark, when it will be taken to his
family in Cambridge to morrow. No accident, that 1 am aware of, happened during the terrible scene.

When Dr. Putnam left, Prof. Webster continued his devotions at intervals, and conversed with considerable freedom, with the officers. ST. CROIX AVIS. Christianstetl, 3d October 1850. We regret much to learn that on Tuesday morning last, the 1st instant, about 2 o'clock, a lire broke out in the town ol Frederiksted, in Queens Street, at the house belonging to and occupied by Miss Eliza Jacobsen and family. On the alarm being given, the people hastened to the spot, and rushing into the house, found the inmates asleep þÿ unconscious of their perilous situation. They were with much difficulty rescued, and not a moment was left them to save the furniture and other things in the house. The adjacent house, occupied by Miss Newcome and family, also took lire, and was partly burnt ; everything in the house was destroyed 5 the rooms in the yard were totally consumed by the devouring element. The house 011 the opposite side of the street, belonging to Miss S. Meyer , and occupied by Mr. England and family, also took lire, but was only partly destroyed ; his loss is said to be great. Several other houses took tire from the sparks, but owing to the activity þÿ present persons ol all classes þÿ and prompt assistance of those particularly the women of the poorer class, no greater damage was done. The conflagration lasted about three hours þÿ the house where the fire originated was burnt to the ground.

TRANSLATION Of the Governor's reply to the Memorial addressed him by the Committee, 011 sending in the Petition to His Majesty, as also of the communication to the Police Magistrate, therein alluded to ; together with the Supplemental Petition that ensued.

Duplicate and Triplicate duly verified that, the original has been sent in, of the most humble Petition of 23d instant, from a number of inhabitants of Christiansted, to Uis Majesty, as to the Provisional Rescript of 30th July last, concerning the right of trade, is hereby officially returned you according to order. The original will be forwarded to the Ministry, together with the necessary elucidations. Respecting the request that the rescript he allowed to lie dormant until His Majesty's most gracious pleasure, in regard to the memorial, may be received, it is hereby officially notified that, the Governor, from what is advanvanced in the Petition, finds no cause of allowing the Rescript to lie dormant. A number of the inhabitants of Frederiksted, some time back, applied personally to the Governor, respecting the approaching alterations, in the existing unwarrantable freedom of trade: the inhabitants of Cliristiansted, however, without the least application to the higher local authority have believed it more suitable to endeavour, by complaint to superior authority, getting the aforesaid rescript rescinded. The Governor, on this occasion, finds himself induced to assure you and your constituents, that complaints to higher authority will not cause him to depart from measures which on mature consideration, he may conceive necessary for the welfare of the colony. Regarding certain points in the Rescript aforesaid, which is considered to be misunderstood ; there is herewith

sent you a copy of a communication, of this day's date, to the Police-Magistrate. Secretary's Office, St. Croix 28th September 1850. (Signed) F. E. ELBERLING. To Messrs. J. M. Johnson. J. v. Beverhoudt. Canvane.

AS it lias come to my knowledge that, some of the Regulations in the Provisional Rescript of 30th July last, have occasioned misunderstandings, I have deemed it suitable ere the Rescript goes into operation on the 1st of October, to communicate the following accessary rules, which are to be observed in tiie application of the Rescript aforesaid. J.) As under the idea of trade, those eases are not included, where anyone in person, or by menials, carry about for sale the products of his or her own industry; and as bread must be considered as appertaining to such products, it is therefore considered as a sequence of what is decreed in % 10 of the Rescript, that every one, as well in town as in the country, is entitled, in person, or by bis servants, to sell, or have carried about for sale, the products of his own industry, and Bread þÿ to their customers. It is only in such cases where the selling is carried on by itinerant sellers, that the sale of the products of one's industry and bread is prohibited in the country and renders a permit necessary for a sale thereof in the Towns. 2.) Conformable to the general rules of trade, every authorised trader in the towns is entitled, in person, to carry about bis goods, from house to house in the town in which he lives. 3.) The rule in >3, that all persons in the towns are entitled to sell, in his or her dwelling, Bread, Candles, Ac. Ac. is also valid for the public markets, where every body is entitled to sell the articles aloresaid.

It being my wish that every one who proves by the execution of this Rescript of 30th July last, his being deprived his sole or main support, may, as far as possible, obtain a suitable recompense, the Police-Magistrate is enjoined, in rigidly attending to the observance of this Rescript, to direct his attention to such especial and particular instances, and to make a due report thereof. Government of ihc Danish Westindia Islands, 8t. Croix 28th September 1850. (Signed) P. HANSEN.

F. E. Elberlino. To the Police Magistrate ofChristiansted. A correct copy, (Signed) Carl Reimer. þÿ þÿs»000«« (T RANSLATI O N.) TO THE KING ! The undersigned as representatives of several hundred inhabitants of the town of Christiansted sent the local Government, the attached most humble Petition, concerning the Provisional Rescript which was issued on the 30th of July last concerning the right of trailing Ac. Ac., and at the same time took the liberty of addressing a memorial, hereunto affixed sub No. 1, soliciting that the aforesaid rescript might lie dormant until Your Majesty's pleasure regarding

our humble prayer could be ascertained. Instead of a complying answer which we had hoped for, both from the encroaching and dangerous nature of the regulations, and the very doubtful competency of the Government stepping forward as lawgiver, in so important an affair, we have received a reply of the 28th instant, here adjoined sub. No. 2, wherein we are informed that the Governor finds 110 inducement to allow the rescript to lie dormant. Far more than the refusal has it surprised us, in seeing, that the Governor considers the stop which we have taker, as an affront giving him an occasion cf assuring 11s and our constituents, "that complaints to superior authority will not induce him to depart from measures which, on mature consideration, he may conceive necessary for the welfare of the colony." Firstly, wc most humbly dare take as granted that, wc are entitled to apply directly to Your Majesty, whenever we find cause of complaint, even against the Governor himself, which, in this instance, we believe to have, in a very high degree occasion for. In the next place þÿ speaking most mildly þÿ we must view the Governor's comparing himself and office to Your Majesty, to whom we have applied, and who is probably meant by " superior authority," as highly improper. In respect to Government, in its communication, denoting the liberty of trade, hitherto existing, as devoid of legal authority; we, on the other hand dare opine that, it is legalised in the rescript of I81I1 April 1834 2 which refers to a

condition and advancement of that kind of trade, not. positively defined but practically established, and as a sequence of that state of things which we have depicted in our principal Petition. With 'lie Government's communication we were simultaneously sent a copy of a communication to the Police Magistrate of Christinnstcd, which we presume to annex sub No. 3, and whereon we will take the liberty of making a few observations. The 3rd $ of the "Provisional Rescript" establishes that, every one in his own dwelling is entitled to sell bread and candles Ac. Twenty passes for the selling of these articles are only to be issued in Christianstnd, and Twelve in Frederiksted, " with this exception,'' says 4 " all trade by itinerant selling is prohibited both in the country and in the town." These regulations, devoid of any thing further, appear to prohibit all traffic that docs not take place within the dwelling of the trader. The Government, meanwhile in its communication No. 1 and 2, has interpreted it thus ; " That every one as well in town as in the country is entitled in person or by servants, to sell, or have carried about for sale, to bis customers, articles, the fruits of bis own industry, and bread," also, " that, public markets, in accordance to the rescript's 3rd are svnonimes for dwelling®."

The reason the Government gives for this interpretation þÿ for it is expressly so denominated, and not modifications þÿ is incomprehensible to us, for $ 10 to which this is referable, has not the least connection with the regulation of the town population, but only concerns "the rural population and the Planters," and does not even name bread, neither could it, where mention is only made of what the rural population may sell in the towns, and assuredly no bread has ever been sold in the towns which has been baked in the country ; but on the contrary bread is generally carried from the towns into the country. INeither can we comprehend the grounds for the enlarged interpretation, that, the public markets are synonimes for dwellings. In No. 2 of this communication, there is found quite another interpretation of 4 and 7, as they deduce from the general prescripts of commercial law, " of every trader being entitled, personally, to carry goods about, from house to house, in the town that he lives in." That it is therefore a necessary sequence of every trader being empowered to employ his clerks or menials, to do whatever work he may himself execute. Ily trade in dwellings, in respect to bread, is consequently to be understood a trallic by menials both out of doors and in the markets, and as regards the vending of all other goods, þÿ the trader, himself, either carrying them about, from door to door, or as sending them by his subordinates. The result, therefore, appears to he

that Government has been pleased, by interpretation, to make void more than a half of its rescript not two months old, so that scarcely any thing remains but the impost. This unwarranted taxation, so contrary to the Ministry's positive order of 2nd July last year, is however one of our chief grounds of complaint. The facility with which Government issues rescripts, and subsequently, by interpretation embodies in them a mean- tagen ved Execution fra Niels C. ing opposite to what may be considered they originally contained, becomes the more dangerous when we take into consideration that every Police Magistrate is appointed under a stipulated understanding of being dismissed whenever the Government becomes dissatisfied with him, and, furthermore when you notice, that the Government's Police- Itescript of last year, denies an appeal of any suit, wherein not more than 6 months labor is adjudged by the Police- Magistrate, so discretionally appointed. VVe are therefore forced to persevere in our most humble Petition, and express our hope that, Your Majesty will cause the entire rescript to be abrogated, and such regulations to be established as can protect the inhabitants against any ill-digested, frivolous, and unwarranted legislation, which we hope may not produce, meanwhile, more want and unhappiness, to the more indigent part of the population.

In respect to whom it is but a sorry consolation, that the Governor in his communication to the Police-Magistrate holds out a kind of promise or expresses a wish of giving a compensation which we have no faith in his being prepared to give, just as little as we consider him entitled to offer it. The incompleteness of the expositions, in these our humble Petitions we pray may be excused in consideration of the brief time given us to frame our complaint. The same reasons constrain us forthwith to send on this our unauthenticated supplemental petition, a copy, whereof, has, however, been sent the Government for explication. Anecdote of BcruadoUc. It was some time during the short peace of 1802 that a foreign gentleman came to Gibraltar with letters of credit and introduction from a mercantile house in Italy to a house of business on the Rock, the ostensible object of this visit being to open transactions between the two firms. The merchant of the Rock having read the letters, received the bearer with cordiality, and made him welcome as an inmate in his house. The foreign merchant, when introduced by his host to the governor, expressed, as much as every stranger, astonishment at the stupendous works, betraying by his observations the most profound ignorance of the science of fortification, and at the same time expressing a natural curiosity to " see the lions," which the governor readily assented to, and introduced him to one of his staff as a Cicerone. The extravagant wonder and puerile observations of the man of commerce at all he saw afforded no small amusement to his conductor, who, after a day or two, tired with doing the civil, allowed the gentleman to rove about among the sentinels, to whom he soon became as familiar as un chien du reginient. The time of departure of the visitant was now close at hand, when one morning the hospitable Gibraltar merchant, who was in the habit of catering for himself, was on his way before breakfast to the fish-market, when he found that in his haste he had put on a wrong hat. On taking it off to examine it he recognised it as the hat of his guest. Something, however, unusual in its ap-

pearance induced him to scrutinize it more closely, when he observed a double crown, concealed in which, to his astonishment, he found plans and elevations, with a most perfect reconnoissance ot the Rock, made by the very simple gentleman who knew not the angle of the flank from the flanked angle of a bastion, nor could tell a " hornwork" from a w" ram's horn." Our Gibraltar merchant, pocketing the papers, hastened to lay the matter before the governor. In the meantime the foreign gentleman, having missed his hat, and suspecting that all was not right, and that by remaining a moment longer he should endanger hispcrsonal liberty, hurried down to the port, and, engaging with a boatman, was beyond the range of the guns of the fortress, and on his way to Cadiz before his friend returned home. The person who thus escaped from the Rock, on his arrival at Cadiz, coolly called on the Itritish Consul, to whom he related the cause of his sudden flight from the British fortress and the loss of his papers and drawings; "but, no matter," said he, pointing to his forehead, 44 I have it all here. 3Iy name is Bernadotte-" It will be remembered that, at St. Helena, Bonaparte mentioned the design he had of laying siege to Gibraltar, with the mode of proceeding and the amount of force to be employed, and the result of which he was confident would have bscn success ; all, no doubt, planned

Petitions have been frequently presented to the French Assembly complaining that the documents and signatures of public functionaries were frequently so ill written as to be illegible. A Ministerial circular has just been issued, declaring that for the future functionaries must write and sign their names plainly, under pain of dismissal.

The French journals state that a petition is being signed at Marseilles praying the National Assembly to pass a law against cursing and swearing: it has already received upwards of 300 signatures. " You have protected animals from ill-treatment," it observes, " and can you permit the name of the Lord to be outraged with impunity in France?" Such a law is in force in England.

A Specimen ol" Transatlantic Persuasion. Mr. Crittenden, an American, was engaged in defending a man who had been indicted for a capital crime. After an elaborate defence, he closed his effort by the following allegory : " When God in his eternal counsel conceived the thought of man's creation, he called to llim the three ministers who wait constantly upon llis throne, Justice, Truth, and Mercy, and thus addressed them : þÿ ' Shall we make man ?' Then said Justice, 4 O ! God, make him not, for he will trample upon thy laws.' Truth made answer also, ' (J ! God make him not, for he will pollute thy sanctuaries.' But Mercy, dropping upon her knees, and looking up through her tears, exclaimed, 4 O ! God, make him ; 1 will watch over him with my care through all the dark paths which he may have to tread." Then God made man, and said to him, 4 O ! man, thou art the child of Mercy ; go and deal with thy brother.'" The jury were affected to tears ; and against the evidence, and what must have been their own convictions, at once brought in a verdict of not guilty. þÿ Mirror of the Time.

YESTERDAY being the anniversary of the birth of our beloved Sovereign King Frederik the Seventh þÿ who on that day completed his 42d year þÿ a royal salute of 27 guns was fired at sun-rise from Fort Christiansvaern, in honor of the happy event. EUROPEAN! TIMES. Liverpool, September 17. DENMARK AND THE DUCHIES. Hamburgh, September 1. þÿ It appears that the Russian fleet has formed a line across the bay of Kiel, having stationed itself, along with some Danish men-ofwar, close to the entrance of the harbour, to prevent any of the Holstein gunboats and steamers leaving their present anchorage. A quantity of heavy artillery has been landed near Eckenforde and Bulk, to the northward of this small fortress, and every day we expect to learn that a movement has taken place along the whole line for the purpose of cannonading that place. The Cologne Gazette has a telegraphic despatch from Frankfort, of the 3rd instant, stating that the Danish Plenipotentiary has summoned the federal committee sitting in that city to ratify the treaty of peace of the 2nd of July.

ST. <0 & O I 31 AT1S. Another despatch from Kiel, of the same date, states that the Holstein Diet has been convoked by the Stadtholders. The Diet is to meet at Kiel, on Monday, the 9th instant. The Cologne Gazette, of the 10th instant, has a telegraphic dispatch from Altona of the 9th, stating that some skirmishing had taken place on the previous day on the whole of the outposts. The left wing of the Ilolsteiners, the ninth and eleventh battalions of foot, and the first regiment were driven back upon Stoderstapel, but being reinforced by another detachment, they advanced again, and forced the Danes back. The centre of the llolstein army has advanced to Jagel, near Schleswig and BreckendorfF, but any further results are not known. It appears from Dresden letters, of the 0th inst., that Austria and those German Governments which stand on her side are preparing to interfere in the Duchies. This, at least, is the meaning of a letter which the Saxon cabinet has addressed to the Stadtholders in reply to their demand that Saxony should, at length, pay the debt she owes to llolstein for the expenses and maintenance of her contingent in 1818. The Bavarian Government had issued a decree, prohibiting subscriptions and collections in aid of the Schlcswi<r-lIolstein cause. Kiel, 9th Sept. þÿ The Legislative Assembly of the Duchies was opened today. Only 00 out of a 100 members were able to attend. The Stadtholder opened the sitting by distinctly announcing the intention of the Government to continue the war. He stated that not-

withstanding their wish to continue at peace hostilities became inevitable, and now that they had commenced, they would not think of entering into any negotiations. As the question was now to be settled by the sword, they must defend their rights by all the means in their power. He explained that the Government had money enough in hand to meet the cost of the army and administration. M. Burgune was then elected President.

DEATH OF LIEUT. GALE THE AERONAUT. The Bordeaux papers contain details of the death of Lieut. Gale, the aeronaut, lie ascended upon the back of a pony, and, at a short distance from the city, made a successful descent. The pony was detached, and, while he was in the act of exhausting the remaining gas his anchor gave way, and the balloon, being relieved of its chief weight, rose suddenly. A tree by which the anchor held snapped, and the shock upset the car. The lieutenant clung to the ropes, and in this state was carried a mile and a quarter, when he dropped, either with the balloon or before it fell. His dead body, with all the limbs broken, was fou i d in a wood. He has left a wife and eight children. He was engaged for twelve nights at .£90 each, free of expense. It is said that the Prefect of þÿ Police in Paris intends to prohibit all

balloon ascents out of the usual mode of performance. þÿ lb. Narvaez has sent the President in return a veritable sword once wielded by Cortez, whom Narvaez claims as an ancestor. þÿ lb.

DESPERATE ATTACK UPON GENERAL IIAYNAU. On Friday morning week, shortly before 12 o'clock, three foreigners, one of whom wore long moustachios presented themselves at the brewery of Messrs. Barclay &, Co., London, for the purpose of inspecting the establishment. According to the regular practice of visitors, they were requested to sign their names in a book in the office, after which they crossed the yard with one of the clerks. On inspecting the visitors' book the clerks discovered that one of the visitors was no other than General Ilaynau, the late commander of the Austrian forces during the Hungarian war. It became known all over the brewery in less than two minutes, and before the general and his companions had crossed the yard nearly all the labourers and draymen were out with brooms and dirt, ' shoutim r> out, " Down with the Austrian butcher," and other epithets of rather an alarming nature to the general. lie was soon covered with dirt, and perceiving some of the men about to attack him ran into the street to Bankside, followed by a large mob, consisting of the brewers' men, coal heavers, and others, armed with all sorts of weapons, with which they belaboured the general, lie ran in a Irantic manner along Bankside until he can e to the George public-house, when forcing the door open he rushed in and proceeded upstairs into one of the bedrooms, to the utter astonishment of Mrs. Benlield the landlady, who soon discovered his name and the reason of his en-

tering her house. The furious mob rushed in alter him, threatening to do for the "Austrian butcher," but fortunately for him the house is very old fashioned and contains a vast number ol doors, which were all forced open except that of the room in which the general was concealed. The mob increased at that time to several hundreds, and Mrs. Benfield became alarmed about her own property as well as the general's life. She accordingly despatched a messenger to the Southwark police station lor the assistance of the police, and in a short time Inspector Squires arrived at the George þÿ with a number of police, and with great difficulty dispersed the mob and got the general out of the house. A police galley was at the wharf at the time, into which he was taken and rowed towards Somerset-house amidst the shouts and execrations of the mob. Messrs. Barclay arc very indignant at the conduct of the men, and no doubt a strict inquiry will be entered into respecting the origin of the attack. þÿ Times.

The Siihinariiic Telegraph hehveeii Calais and Hover. Dover, August 4. þÿ The wire so successfully submerged last week lias been cut asunder among the rocks at Cape Grisnez, where the physical configuration of the French coast has been found unfavorable for it as a place of holdfast or fixture. All communication between coast and coast has consequently been suspended for the present. The precise point where the breakage took place is 200 yards out at sea, and just where the twenty miles of electric line that had been streamed out from Dover joins on to a leaden tube, designed to protect it from the surge beating against the beach, and which serves the purpose of conveying it up the front of the cliff to the telegraph station on the top. The leaden conductor, it would appear, was of too soft a texture to resist the oscillation of the sea, and thereby became detached from the coil of gutta percha wire that was thought to have been safely encased in it. The occurrence was, of course, quickly detected by the sudden cessation of the series of communications which have been sustained since the lirst sinking of the electric cable between jhere and the Cape, though it was at first a perplexing point to discover at what precise spot the wire was broken or at fault. This, however, was done by hauling up Ihe line at intervals, a process which disclosed the gratifying fact that since its first sinking it had remained in situ at the bottom of the sea, in consequence of the leaden weights or clamps that were

strung to it at every sixteenth of a mile. The operation was accomplished by Messrs. Brett, Reid, YVollaston, and Edwards, who have been attending to the management of the telegraph without intermission, and who are now, with their staff, removing the wire to a point nearer Calais, where from soundings it has been ascertained that there are no rocks, and where the contour of the coast is favorable. It is thought that for the present leaden tube a tube of iron must be substituted, the present apparatus being considered too fragile to be permanently answerable. The experiment, as far as it has gone, proves the possibility of the gutta percha wire resisting the action of the salt water, of the fact of its being a perfect waterproof insulator, and that the weights on the wire are sufficient to prevent it being drifted away by the currents, and of sinking it in the sands. During the period that the wire was perfect, messages were daily printed by Brett's Printing Telegraph, in legible Roman type, 011 long strips of paper, in the presence of a numerous French and English audience ; but it is not intended to make use of the wire for commercial and newspaper purposes until the connexion of it with the telegraphs of the South Eastern and that now completed on the other side from Calais to Paris is effected. Should the one wire answer, it is intended eventually to run out twenty or thirty more, so as to have a constant reserve in the event of accident in readiness. This huge reticulation of
electric line will represent 400 miles of telegraph submerged in the sea, and as each will be a considerable distance apart, a total water width of six or eight miles in extent.

An invention has been patented, called the Autographic Press, by which a letter written on prepared paper can be transferred by a short process to a metallic plate, from which any number of copies may afterwards be taken on common paper, and by ordinary pressure.

Submarine Telegraph from Dover to Calais. þÿ On Monday last the remaining portion of the gutta percha tubing, enclosing the wire for the telegraph, was removed from the works of the Gutta Percha Company, Wharf-road, City-road, to Dover, preparatory to being sunk. The whole length of this tubing, which is halt-an-inch in diameter, is about twenty-five miles, and there are five lengths for as many wires. The wires will be sunk by means of leaden weights, at distances of 100 yards. The whole of the works will be completed, it is expected, in about a week, when we shall have instantaneous communication between London and Paris. þÿ (Patent Journal.) with thirty miles of wire, and a wheel or drum of large dimensions upon which to wind il, and so gradually pay it out in proceeding across the Channel. It is expected that this operation will take place þÿimmediately. Globe, of Saturday.

4t Belfast, last week, ayoungman resolved to take a dose of " arsenic" in order to hasten his love-lorn self to that " bourn whence no traveller returns." He dealt, however, with a careful druggist, and, magnesia being a harmless drug, he failed to die. Nevertheless, he made a dying speech and confession whilst racked with the "poison's pains," and so eloquently spoke that he converted the lady from indifference to favour, and secured a bridal, not a death bed.

Get Knowledge. þÿ Pope, the poet, has a line, " a little learning is a dangerous tiling," which we often hear repeated, as a maxim, by those who have but a very little themselves. We have also this other maxim, " half a loaf is better than no bread and this is certainly true of bread. Is it not likely to be true in knowledge also ? Try it in a few practical cases. A little knowledge of navigation is better to the sailor than no knowledge. A little knowledge of soils, and seasons, and cropping, and stock, is better for the farmer than no knowledge. A little knowledge of anatomy is better to the surgeon than no knowledge. The truth is, that much knowledge is the best thing; a little knowledge the next best; and no knowledge the worst of all. The line oC the poet is good in the sound, but bad in the sense.
