EUROPEAN TIMES. Liverpool, September 17. Mr. Josias Booker, a gentleman wellknown through the length and breadth of the West Indies, sailed in his own ship, the John Ilarrocks, for Demerara, on the 4th instant, and will probably have reached his destination before this sheet meets the eyes of many of our more distant colonial readers. Mr. Booker has long had large landed possessions in British Guiana, and, notwithstanding the present depreciated value of West India property, he has very considerably extended his estates during the last two or three years by additional purchases. We mention the fact as the strongest proof of the inherent force of his character. A more timid and less energetic man would have shrunk, in the present condition of West India property, from sinking his capital in the soil. But, like Richelieu, Mr. Booker believes "There's no such word as fail !" He has taken out one of his sons, a fine youth, just blooming into manhood, a few labourers, and a stock of agricultural implements, the most perfect and unique which probably ever left Europe for the tropics. þÿ It is this determination, under the most adverse circumstances, not to yield to despondency, but to make the best of of thinking or devising plans for himself. circumstances, which has always brought out some of the finest traits in the national character. Mr. Booker possesses this national stamina in jierfection. He is the man for an emergeney ; and the experiment on which he is about to enter in the growing of cotton, is of the first importance to the mother

country as well as to the colonists themselves. The power which one energetic mind exercises over others less active is seen in the every day events of life j but this power, acting on a wide field, and directed to a great object, must, when successful, work results of an allimportant character. The task which Mr. looker lias determined to achieve þÿ that of making money out of West India property, and competing with slave countries, þÿ is, no doubt, difficult, and many would regard it as hopeless. But of his success we entertain not the least doubt, for the intelligence of this fine

of his prompt and energetic character. Gratified as we shall be to learn that our friend has exceeded his own expectations, we should rejoice in his success less on personal than on public grounds, because his example would find many brilliant imitators, and the tone of apathy in which it is too customary to speak of the beautiful isles of the West would certainly give way to a more healthy and inspiriting feeling. This is the morale which takes Mr. Booker's efforts out of the ordinary category of private speculation, and induces us to place before our readers the name of a gentleman whose modesty prompts him to shrink from the publicity of his own acts.
Mr. Booker has not to establish his character as a practical planter ; that

ATI 3% has been done years ago. The transactions of the Society of Arts, Manufac- " tures, and Commerce," show what this gentleman has done to economise time and labour under the most disadvantageous circumstances in Demerara. In awarding to Mr. Booker the society's large gold medal, for machinery worked by cattle as a substitute for human labour in the ginning of cotton, the transactions, after showing that the saving of expense amounted to fifty per cent., go on to pay the following tribute to Mr. Booker's improvements and their practical results: "Mr. Booker's wise humanity was not confined within the bounds of the estate committed to his management, but his neighbours had the discernment to see the advantage that he was deriving from it, and the good sense, in several instances, to follow his example. May the good seed that has thus been sown grow and prosper ; and may the society have the satisfaction of bestowing more medals for this object." This is the gist of the whole case þÿ the force of example. Man seems to be an imitative animal. The amount of originality in his composition is marvellously small. He will instinctively follow the best course when it is pointed out to him þÿ when he can follow it mechanically, without the trouble

The exercise of the mind with most men is an effort, and Europeans under a tropical sun can hardly be said to be either mentally or physically improved by the transplanting. In the case of a sturdy robust intellect, that dares any danger in the pursuit of an object þÿ sacrifices every luxury to be useful to his species þÿ gives up all the endearments of a home, a handsome private fortune, and the gratification of the refined tastes which throw a charm around the homesteads of England, þÿ the work of improvement becomes a labour of love, and the stimulating effects of a noble ambition are seen in the number of imitators which success calls into existence. If a majority ef landed proprietors in the West Indies had possessed a tithe of the indomitable spirit and enterprise which has marked Mr. Booker's connexion with Demerara, it is not exaggerating to say that the prospects specimen of a British merchant is worthy of the islands would be brighter than at present. Instead of calling on the Government for help, they should have helped themselves, þÿ for heaven and humanity conspire to aid and respect those who aid themselves. Mr. Booker is deeply embued with the injustice which has been done to the West Indies, but it has not prevented him from trusting to his own resources to overcome the physical and moral obstacles which stand in the way of West Indian progression. If all improvement is to cease until the British Government concede all that the colonists demand, the Greek Kelends

will have arrived. The high political and social standing of Mr. Booker in his native country, causes his return to it to be viewed with extreme interest by the troops of friends who rejoice in his friendship. Of the

feeling with which his family look forward to such an event it is needless here to speak. The length of his absence will be regulated, in all probability, by the ratio of his success ; for he is not a man to do things by halves. But that he may return, triumphant in his aspirations, to delight the society in which he moves and to say to the owners of West India property in the mother country, " Go thou and do like wise," is the wish of all who know the estimable qualities of the gentleman in whose mission, on account of its moral intrepidity and nobleness, we confess we take a deep and abiding interest.

FRANCE. The President's Visit to Ciiekboi lid. þÿ The President's visit to Cherbourg appears to have been very cool and very polite. The cries of " Vive la Republique" were general, those of " Vive Napoleon," or " Vive le President," were few and far between. Ti e temper of the good citizens had been a little soured by the delay which took place in the arrival of the great man, who entered the city near dusk, after all the national guards had been for hours under arms expecting him, and were necessarily jaded, hungry, and inclined to be peevish. The following is a description of what followed when he did come : þÿ " A flash, followed by a loud report from a gun on the heights of the town, announced the long expected arrival. The fire was taken up by the batteries, which soon filled the air with their thunder, w hile the sky was lighted every instant from the cannon's mouth. In a few minutes a few gensdarmerie passed through the lines of the soldierv at a sling trot ; then came a squadron of the 1st dragoons, fine looking fellow s with bearskin helmets and leopard skin mountings, red-faced coats, and red pantaloons of preposterous dimesions ; and at last the President, preceded by a mounted linktnau, appeared in an open carriage, attended by the Ministers and follow ed by carriages with his suite, as well as by an escort, some few calcches, and a considerable number of the municipality and of rural mayors." In the evening the President dined with the Prefect. The following day

(Friday week) he reviewed the troops. A grand banquet followed, at which 5000 persons were present. The Earl of Wilton, the Duke of Marlborough, the Earl of Cardigan, and several other distinguished English gentlemen, who had arrived in their own yachts, were present. The owners of the yachts present had arranged to present the visitors a species of entertainment perfectly new to the French, and w hich none but Englishmen have the means for displaying, namely, a cruise of all their handsome yachts, accompanied by a variety of beautifully-executed manoeuvres out of the bay, at one extremity of the great breakwater, which they worked round, returning by the other again to mantcuvre in the bay, to the great delight and surprise of the French of both sexes, who could hardly credit that such a

scientific display of seamanship could be made, even in a Liliputian lleet, by men not all of the naval profession. The manner of executing their evolutions, and getting up to their anchorage in two lines, gave so much satisfaction that they were loudly cheered by the people of the port. The captain of the French line-of-battle ship Gemmappes avowed his admiration by exclaiming that the display of their prowess and tactics was " Superbe et t res-delicieuse." On Sunday the President visited all the ships of war, witnessed their manoeuvres, and a grand dinner was afterwards given to the chief officers of the squadron, who were also joined by the Admirals Napier, Cochrane, and Lyons, and several other English officers. The President's toast to the French tleet was greatly applauded. The President left Cherbourg o at ten on Monday a «, morning. o It is said that General Changarnier will put down by force any attempts at a Bonapartist demonstration in honour of the President's return to Paris. Some disturbances took place on the 4th instant at Cliouslct, in the department of the Drome, in consequence of an attempt to prevent some arrests. þÿ The national guards of a neighbouring canton, showing a disposition to assist in rescuing the prisoners, the general of the division has ordered their disarmament, and has given orders for a prompt suppression of the riot. Trade in Paris is more brisk than usual for the season. The accounts from the agricultural districts are more favourable, although the

jiotato disease is making further progress, and the corn markets generally show a downward tendency. Silk has further declined. It is feared that the vintage will be very inferior. The Councils-General continue to vote for a revision of the constitution.

Accounts from Algeria state that the cholera had ceased at Bona, and broken out at Biscara, where it attacked dogs, fowls, and other animals with the same violence as human beings. Several officers of distinction, amongst whom is the commandant of Biscara, have fallen victims to the malady. It was, however, believed that the period of its disappearance was near at hand. Paris, Thursday. þÿ The President continued to be received with enthusiasm in all the places he passed through on his way to Paris. The hour of his entry into the capital would be concealed as much as possible, to prevent any manifestations.

The Times calls in question altogether the utility of these establishments, at, least in a great number of instances: þÿ " We should be greatly edified if some one would explain to us the mysteries of state which at this moment, or at any moment, may occupy the mind of our worthy representative at Stuttgart, for example, or at any one of the German states. Why should there be at every petty court a sort of court gossip writer

3 V? , 8 Ut t> I X A T 3 3. þÿ collector ot idle scandal, a reporter wbose duty it is to pry into all the intrigues, whether of love or politics, and despatch a scandalous chronicle by every post to our Foreign Office ? Where a court exists, there we seem to think a minister necessary, simply because we've never asked ourselves the question þÿ for what object is a minister needed? Have we commercial relations at Stuttgart, or Munich even, which require investigation ? Are there at this moment questions of difference between the courts of Bavaria and England which require to be settled? If there be, let them be immediately stated and arranged ; but do not let the money of the English people, earned at the expense of many hours of toil, and more of anxiety and sorrow, be wasted in the idle folly called diplomatic intercourse. The state mysteries are but a blind to hide idleness; there is, in fact, nothing to do ; but there are people who want to be paid for doing nothing."

Wasting tiie Navy Estimates. Some two or three weeks since we directed public attention to the waste of money voted for the navy estimates, in ordering between £4000 and 5000 to be spent in repairing her Majesty's eightgun brig Ferret, a class of ships entirely superseded by our small steamers, threefourths of one of which could be built new for about the money ordered to be wasted on the Ferret. We have now to record another act of extravagant folly on the part of the Admiralty. Upon a report of the defective condition of the Alecto steamer, their lordships' ordered a committee of master shipwrights to assemble at Woolwich to re-survev the vessel. They met, and condemned her as not worth the money required to repair her; and, upon this decision, their lordships' ordered the works to be suspended. A few days afterwards, however, the Admiralty altered their mind, and, in their wisdom, they have since determined that she shall be repaired at a cost to the navy estimates of between £5000 and £0000. These sums it must be understood, are first estimates. As in the cases of the Vanguard, Superb, Collingwood, and others, we have no doubt that we shall have supplemental estimates of about half as much more to be expended upon them before they arc out of hand. This is dockyard economy Avith a vengeance. If this useless extravagance is to be perpetuated, the continual waste of our income-tax money on rotten and worthless-ships, the sooner we have another turn out or reform the better, for it appears that
running from Symonds to Walker is lit eially jumping out of the frying-pan into the fire.

The Importance ol'llic Reniilifiil. What are half the crimes in the world committed for? What brings into action the best virtues ? The desire, of possessing. Of possessing what ? Not mere money, but every species of the beautiful which money can purchase. A man lies

hid in a little, dirty, smoky room for twenty years of his life, and sums up as many columns of figures as would reach round half the earth, if they were laid at length ; he gets rich ; what does he do with his riches? lie buys a large wellproportioned house ; in the arrangement of his furniture he gratifies himself with all the beauty which splendid colours, regular figures, and smooth surfaces can convey ; he has the beauties of variety and association in his grounds ; the cup out of which he drinks his tea is adorned with beautiful figures ; the chair in which he sits is covered with smooth shining leather ; his table-cloth is of the most beautiful damask ; mirrors reflect the lights from every quarter of the room ; pictures of the best masters feed his eye with all the beauties of imitation. A million of human creatures are employed in this country in ministering to this feeling of the beautiful. It is only a barbarous, ignorant people that can ever be occupied by the necessaries of life alone. If to eat, and to drink, and to be warm, were the only passions of our minds, we should all be what the lowest of us are at this day. The love of the beautiful calls man to fresh exertions, and awakens him to a more noble life ; and the glory of it is, that as painters imitate, and poets sing, and statuaries carve, and architects rear up the gorgeous trophies of their skill, and as every thing becomes beautiful, and orderly, and magnificent, the activity of the mind rises to still greater and to better

objects. The principles of justice are sought out; the powers of the ruler and the rights of the subject are fixed ; man advances to the enjoyment of rational liberty, and to the establishment of those great moral laws which God has written in our hearts, to regulate the destinies of the world.

Give me, for a beautiful sight, a neat and smart woman, heating her oven and setting in the bread ! And, if the bustle does make the sign of labour glisten on her brow, where is the man that would not kiss that off, rather than lick the plaster from'a duchess.

The Sen-Serpeiil oil Kerry. " Many a time and oft," of late, have we chronicled the movements of the Great Sea-serpent. With a solicitude surpassing both in devotion and pertinacity that with which Dickon's detective friends track their thievish prey we have followed the great Unknown's career; not as they, to punish crimes, for none are laid to our quarry's charge, (save contempt of Professor Owen,) but solely and simply from a desire to announce the existence of a new wonder on the earth. Again and again have we fondly imagined that we had him, " at length", that at last all doubt would be dispelled from the long told talc of his beiti" u O ' : that, " in the last resort," to use Can-

nine's phrase, we might in disputably succeed in transfixing him, not with "flic arrows of contempt" and scepticism, hut with one of those veritable harpoons which demonstrate to marine monsters that they are in one respect at least, " very like a whale," namely, mortal. But, no! Often as the Unknown had been announced, deep in the tropic ocean buried did he remain ; conceiving, apparently, that with " Cape" to the south, "Madeira" to the north, and " St. Helena" by his side, he possessed a berth not to be abandoned upon any trifling occasion and at every passing desire. Wearied out, we at last almost abandoned hope, and resolved to settle down under the conviction, that to us at least the tale of the Sea-serpent would not be unfolded ; resolving to exclude him, henceforth, from our columns, as guilty of contempt. But, whether from the heat of the summer at home, from ennui, or from any other imaginable cause, the Leviathan has again unexpectedly saluted us. Last week we reported him far distant at sea : now we record him on our own shores ; gambolling with zest amid the cool waters of the Kerry coast, and kicking up such a marine dust, so to say, as not improbably may raise St. Patrick and call down upon his curiously-formed head a sentence of banishment like that which the venerable saint once denounced upon the monsters' kith and kin ashore. "Better late than never," is, however, a true adage, and, whilst expressing our own welcome to the Unknown, with a hope for his better acquaintance, let

us indicate our trust, that, although the Serpent has, unhappily, come just too late to join the British Association, Professor Owen and his friends will be prepared to play the host in the best style, and induce the great stranger to take up his quarters, permanently, in regions less secluded and outlandish than those he has so graciously quitted for the edification of the scientific world. þÿ Liveerrooi. (from a liverpooi, paper.) Mice. þÿ A sudden influx of mice into a house, hitherto free from their ravages, © denotes approaching mortality among its inhabitants. A mouse running over a person is considered to be an infallible sign of death ; as is, also, the squeaking of one behind the bed of an invalid, or ihe appearance or apparition of a white mouse running across the room. To meet with a shrew-mouse in going a journey is reckoned ominous of evil. þÿ The country people have an idea that the harvest-mouse is unable to cross a path which has been trod by man. þÿ Whenever they attempt they are immediately, as my informant expressed it, " struck dead." This, they say, accounts for the numbers which on a summer's evening may be found lying dead on the verge of the field footpaths, without any external wound or apparent cause for their demise.

Bees. þÿ The superstitious ceremonies and observances attached to these animals appear to be current throughout the kingdom, and by no means suffer a diminution in this county. Among others of less common occurrence, we have the belief that they will not thrive in a quarrelsome family. The wild, or, as we term him, the humble, bee is not without a share of the superstitions which pertain to his more civilized brethren. The entrance of one into a cottage is deemed a certain sign of death.
Spiders. þÿ The small spiders called " money-spiders" prognosticate good luck ; in order to propitiate which they must be thrown over the left shoulder.

So, it seems that Mr. Clayton and the present cabinet are determined to have a war, that is if we believe them, with some foreign power, and that Spain is the one selected. Several of the organs of the cabinet in this metropolis, made t!ie announcement yesterday, detailing the positive information that the Secretary of State regards a rupture with Spain almost unavoidable, in consequence of the disputed questions growing out of the recent invasion of Cuba, under the command of Lopez and his pirates, or, patriots, as the case may be. In the Tribune, we find the following despatch : þÿ PROBABLE WAR BETWEEN SPAIN AND THE UNITED STATES. Washington, Friday June 14. The Secretary of State has received despatches from General Campbell, our Cons il at Havana, informing the gov- : eminent that tire Count of Alcoy (Governor General of Cuba) peremptorily refuses to surrender the þÿC ontroy prisoners, although proof was clear that they sh pped for Chagrcs, without an intent of participating in 1 lie expedition. Mr. Clayton has despatched instructions to General Campbell to make an unqualified demand for the prisoners, and, in the event of another refusal, war will be declared against Spain. Mr. Bulwer has given assurances that England will not interfere, considering the course of the United States, thus far, unexceptionable. Mr. Clayton now evidently regards a ; rupture with Spain as unavoidable. If this singular announcement appear-

ed in the Tribune alone the editor of w Inch is in Washin gton, we might, out of pure charity, consider it a revival of the celebrated Slievegammon intelligence, which was communicated through the same channel, during the attempted revolution in Ireland, about a year ago. But this intelligence comes to us from Washington, not on Slievegammon authoriiy alone. It is corroborated, to a very considerable extent, by a more cautious, but equally warlike, announcement in the Courier and Enquirer, of which the following are the principal points, the one corroborating the other as to what the cabinet would like to do, had they the power : important from CUBA. We have private advices by telegraph, from our Washington correspondent, which represent the condition of our relations with Cuba as being less satisfactory than has been reported hitherto. Despatches have been received at the State department, from Mr. Campbell, our Consul at Havana, by the steamer Isabel, dated June 8th in which he states that the captains of the Georgiana and the Sarah Loud will probably be executed by the Spanish authorities, unless the United States government immediately and peremptorily interferes. The other prisoners, it was believed, would be treated with less severity. This was

3 tr. © ® © i » a?is. the impression not only of the consul, but of the American shipmasters and oihers in Havana. 3Ir. Campbell asks for positive instructions, peremptorily to demand the surrender of the prisoners, fearing that no other interference would have any effect. The tenor of his despatches leads our correspondent to infer that, at the time they were written, Mr. Campbell had not received Mr. þÿClayton s instructions of the 1st inst. The summarial process against the prisoners had not closed at the date of Mr. þÿCampbell s letters. All the proceedings were kept secret, not withstanding the rumours that have been circulated to the contrary. It was understood that the trials would be conducted in strict accordance with the rigid process of the Spanish law. The fate of the prisoners, was, of course, uncertain unless Mr. þÿClayton sdespatches should be received before the matter was closed ; their tone and tenor could hardly fail to have some effect upon the Spanish authorities. The Spanish minister has not been seen since the arrival of the Isabel ; his views, and the tenor of despatches he may have received, are therefore unknown. The aspect of affairs is still a little threatening. The administration is disposed and determined to hold the Cuban authorities to the most rigid accountability for any injury they may inflict upon American citizens not guilty of participation in the invasion. The next despatches from Mr. Campbell w ill be looked for with deep anxiety. Thus, then, on the authority of the

cabinet, and circulated by the organs of the cabinet, we are informed of almost the positive certainty that a war with Spain must grow out of the recent complicated affairs between the United States and the Cuban authorities, that is if we are to believe them, and one of those organs goes so tar as to say, that the administration is determined to declare war, without reference to the disposition or action of Congress. In this, however, they go a little too fast ahead. Neither the President nor the cabinet has any power under the constitution to declare war, no matter how muchsoever they may, for their own purposes, be inclined to do so, without the previous sanction and concurrence of Congress. þÿ The It is very true that Mr. Polk, in bringing on the war with Mexico, took almost the whole responsibility of that event on his own shoulders: but he was aided and assisted by the audacity, folly, and impertinence of the Mexican military authorities on the Itio Grande. The Mexicans made the attack, and General Taylor, the commander of the American troops on the border, was put on the defensive ; and the two countries were involved in war without any previous declaration sanctioned by Congress. It is doubtful if Spain will give the Galphin cabinet such a chance. In the event of a rupture between the Spanish authorities in Cuba, and the United States, growing out of our present difficulties, we þÿcan perceive, t how-

ever, how war can grow out of it, without its first being authorized By Congress, and a debate and discussion had upon it in the old and regular way. þÿ Perhaps, however, Mr. Clayton and the Galphin cabinet intend to intimate the policy of Mr. Polk, in bringing on the Mexican war ; and if we are to believe their organs, they have already made up their minds to bring about a collision between Spain and the United States, on their own responsibility, and without the previous sanction or concurrence of Congress, or without Spain, or the Spanish authorities in Cuba, giving any occasion for it. It may be done, too þÿ but smart as the cabinet are, in their own estimation, we hardly think they will have an opportunity þÿ but if such an event should be the result of the present complication of affairs, all the technical questions arising under the treaty, or the laws of 1813, will be entirely set aside, and the whole impulse and soul of the nation will be given to carrying on the war, with the same force as was that with Mexico. If the nations of Lurope should be þÿneutral we mean France and þÿEngland and allow the United States and Spain to fight it out, there can be little doubt of the result of the contest. In less than six months, all the authority of Spain in Cuba, and Porto Hico, would be entirely annulled and set aside. A great deal of danger and damage, however, would ensue, in the mean time, to the commerce of this country, which is scattered over every sea and ocean in the world.

In the opinion of the cabinet in Washington, this might be compensated by keeping them in power. After all, however, this may be only another of the curious, sudden, and extraordinary movements which characterized Mr. Clayton during the past year, and on a par with that in connection with France. We were on the eve of a war with that country for a whole week, in consequence of the quarrel between him and M. Poussin, and this pronounciamento, through the cabinet organ, may be a repetition of the farce. -- «- TELEGRAPHIC. Boston, May 20, 1850. Brig Enoch, Benner, arrived today, from Port au Prince, with dates to May 2d. The Albany, Germantown and Vixen, were in port. The special agent of the United State s Mr. Benji. E. Green, had an interview with the Emperor Soulouque, in which he demanded the recognition of our commercial agent, and that he shall have the same privileges as those of other nations. He also demanded the appointment of a person to confer with him on certain claims lie had to present against the government, and Gen. l)elvio, a black, was appointed. The cause of the United States government coming forward with their claims, at the present time, is unknown. The Germantown and Albany were short of provisions, and were to have sailed immediately for home. The latter is bound for this port.

Evil Speaking. þÿ It is not good to speak evil of all whom we know to be bad ; it is worse to judge evil of any one who may prove good. To speak ill upon knowledge shows a want of charity ; to speak ill upon suspicion shows a want of honesty. I will not speak so had as I know of many ; I will not speak so bad as I know of any. To know evil of others, and not speak of it, is sometimes discretion. To speak evil of others, and not know it, is always dishonesty. He may be evil himself who speaks good of others upon knowledge ; but he can never he good himself who speaks evil of others on suspicion.

Physiognomy is generally looked upon as an idle science, not, indeed, deserving the name. All must admit that it is an uncertain one ; but yet there is something in the human countenance, whether it he in feature or expression, or in both combined, which has its effect upon every one. We judge by it, even when we know not that we are judging ; we act in consequence of its indications, without being aware that we are influenced by it.

ST. CROIX AVIS, Christ iaiistod, July 25, 1850. We give below a brief summary of some of the most important news by ti e 1st July Packet. The Danish Consul at Hamburgh bar published a notice, that every captain of a vessel sailing under the Danish flag must, on his arrival in that bailout, report himself at His consulate within twenty-four hours ; under a penalty of 50 thalcrs. The shots said to have been fired at the Danish vessels on the coast of Schleswig were from a land battery on the Fehmar Sound. The ships were approaching the shore within the distance allowed, and a blank charge was fired as a signal to show their colors. As this was not done, and they continued to near the coast, a second shot was fired with bull. The vessels were out of the range of the pieces, and no notice was taken of the firing. They both stood out again to sea. The strength of the Danish force in the island of Alsen is estimated at from 10,000 to 18,000 men. Her Majesty the Queen of England was assailed by an individual by name Robert Pate, whilst she was paying a visit to her illustrious relative, the Duke of Cambridge, and while the carriage was within the gates of Cambridgehouse, lie aimed a blow at her face, which took effect upon her cheek, and crushed her bonnet over her forehead. Her Majesty was so little hurt that she was ahie 1<> appear at the opera in the course of the evening. The offender is the son of a man of considerable fortune, has moved in a respectable sphere of society, and held the commission of Lieut, in the regiment of 10th Hussars.

A serious accident occurred to Sir Robert Peel on the evening of June 29, as he was entering into Grosvenor-placc, on Constitution Iiill. He was riding, and his horse suddenly shied at something that was passing, and kicking up its heels, threw him down. The hon.
baronet was taken up insensible and carried borne. Alter a careful examination had been made the following bulletin was issued : þÿ

" Sir Robert Peel has met with a severe accident by falling from his horse. There is severe injury of one shoulder, with a fracture of the left collar bone. þÿ There is great reason to hope that there is no internal injury." The King of Prussia performed the ceremony of laying the first stone of the monument to be erected in the grounds of the Invalids, to the memory of t lie Prussian soldiers and officers who fell " for King and Fatherland" in the revolutionary conflict of the years 1848 and 1849. It was the first time he had appeared in public since the attempt on his Council life. The Crown Prince of Sweden has returned with his royal consort, and was well received by the royal family and a great multitude of people.

From the St. Thomas Times, July 20, 1S50 By the courtesy of the Company's Superintendent at this port, we have been favored with a copy of the New Plan of Mail Routes, which will commence from Southampton 011 Friday the 2nd day of August 1850, and from which we now proceed to give our readers a few extracts, so far as St. Thomas will be concerned. Ac., from the other steamers, and start 6 a. m., on the 18th at and 3rd of each month lor Southampton direct. Route 2. þÿ A steamer will leave St. Thomas at 6 a. m., on the 20lh of each month for Porto Rico, Jamaica, Vera Cruz, and Tampico ; returning to St. Thomas by 1 a. in., on the 17th of each month, with Mails for the Home steamer of the 18th, and also to receive Mails from the out steamer of the 19th of each month, when this No. 2 ship will proceed to do this route over again. Route 3. þÿ A steamer will leave St. Thomas at 6 a. 111., on the 5th of eacli month, for Porto Rico, Jacmel, Jamaica, Havana, and Honduras ; returning to St. Thomas by midnight on the 1st of each month, with Mails for the Home steamer
of the 3rd, and also to receive Mails from the out steamer of the 4th of each month, . when this No. 3 Steamer will proceed to I 1110ns, which left Barbadoes along with perform this route over again.

It will lie seen that St. Thomas will receive its outward Mails 011 the 19th and 4th ot each month, the homeward steamers starting from St. Thomas 011 the 18th and 3rd of each month, giving 14 days for preparing replies to each mail. St. Thomas will have a fortnightly communication, both ways, with all places to windward, Jamaica, Porto Rico, Carthagena, Chagres, Ac. ; and a monthly communication with Mexico, Havana, Honduras, and Nassau ; the communication being cut oft' altogether with Bermuda, La Guayra, and Porto Cabcllo. As regards La Guayra, we believe the good folks down there have themselves to thank for it, as they have at all times

done everything in their power to annoy the Company, and tiring outrageous char- " ges against the line little packet vessel Larne." The periods fixed for departing from the several Termini, as stated in the tables, will lie adhered to ; and if, 011 the return voyages, the steamers should fail to accomplish the speed estimated (9 knots per hour, throughout,) the time so lost must be retrieved, if possible, by curtailing the subsequent stoppages. \\ hen the several steamers assembled at St. Thomas shall have coaled, exnecessary changed Mails, and completed all the j will be brought on here, in the ('011 transfers, Ac., they are to proceed to their respective destinations, without further delay, although the time of stoppage stated "in the tables should not have expired, it being most important that the delivery of Her Britanic Majesty's Mails should lie expedited as much as possible. Although 110 alterations can be made in the Routes, without permission of Her in cases of accident to any of the (except Britanic Majesty's Government, ships,) still the Company's Superintendents abroad are authorised to change the vessels when they deem it necessary. The "Clyde" steamer, Captain Moss, whichleft Southamptonon the 17th June, made a line run to linrhudocs, having reached that place on the 7th July, where she met the Medway and Eagle; afterwards starting on the 10th July for St. 1 liomas, 011 which voyage she met with very heavy weather, and was struck with lightning when lying to between Santa

Cruz and St. Thomas on the night of the 12th July, but fortunately the only injury lant done was the shivering the fore topgal- mast to pieces. She reached the harbour about 9a. 111., on the 13th, and was prevented from completing coal, by the state of the weather, until noon 011 the 14th, when she started for Jacmel and Jamaica. The "Medway" steamer, Captain Sythe Clyde, met with still heavier weather, I

all along the Islands, having communicated with much difficulty at some, omitting Guadaloupe altogether, and bringing on several passengers to St. Thomas bound for the different Islands. In fact there has been a regular hurricane in the neighbourhood of the Windward Islands, which seems to have touched St. Lucia, Martinique, Dominica, Guadeloupe, Antigua, Montserrat, Nevis, St. Martins, St. Kitts, Ac., passing 011 towards the north. At Antigua the barometer fell to 29. 10. Several fine ships an blown 011 shore, or had to cut away their masts, at St. Kitts, St. Martins, Antigua, Ac. The Medway went through all the rough weather in fine style, arriving here 011 the 14th, but too late to get ready for England, as was at first intended, fin- Dee having such a very heavy freight of specie, Ac., to transfer. The Medway remains in our port till the 23rd July, when she will proceed to Porto Rico, on her return to coaling, and proceeding at noon on the 31st instant for Bermuda, and Southampton, with all the Home Mails, Ac. The steamer Dec, Captain Allan, met some of the bad weather off Porto Rico, but arrived here on the 13th, with $ 1,500, (KM) in specie, and otherwise a large freight for England ; and started at noon on the 15th, for Southampton, with about 75 passengers. The "Larne," Captain Sawyer, arrived here from the Main 011 the I4tli, and proceeded r.ext day to Porto Rico with þÿ Mails ex-Clyde, returning to this port on the 18th instant. She nil! remain here till the 23rd July, when she will start

for La Guayra and Porto Cabello, with the out Mails of the 2nd July. This will be the last trip made by any of the Company's vessels to this part of the Spanish Main, as the Company have found the route not worth keeping a vessel on, and the Government have allowed this mail line to be abandoned altogether. On the Larnes' return to St. Thomas, about the 12th of August, she will remain here till the 3rd September, when she will proceed with the Mails, 011 the new Nassau route. The steamer "Great Western" would leave Southampton on the 2nd Julv, the last ship for Bermuda; and her Mails way steamer, about the 23rd July: the latter vessel proceeding along the Windward Islands, in a few hours after her arrival. The steamer "Eagle," ('apt. Rosterrick, may he looked for here about the 36th instant, from Barbadoes and the Windward Islands.

To tiii; Editor of the St. Croix Avis. Dear Sir, 1 here are four Christian Churches existing here. '1 he doctrine of the Trinity is a fundamental doctrine in each of them, ihese Churches have recently heen attacked by the zealous circulation of Swedenborg's books, and the Pamphlets and Tracts of his Apologists, in which the doctrine of the Trinity as held by them, has been assailed and þÿdenied together with other fundamental doctrines of the Apostles creed ; and last week I sow with regret, that the columns of your valuable paper, were opened for the dissemination of these errors and renewed attacks npon the faith of these Churches. It was on account of these things and because the communication replied to contained an erroneous assertion which 1 believed to have originated with Swedenborg, together with a statement of a Trinity that would be satisfactory to the writer evidently drawn from Swedenborg's writings that I was induced to pass by the anonymous writer, and allude directly to the errors of Swedenborg himself. It moreover scented to me a grievously wicked thing, the attempt to unsettle the faith of individuals by the circulation of objections to the Trinity, that have been again and again answeted and refuted, and this especially in a community, where hundreds are just beginning to read and inquire, and who have hi fhcrto been unaccustomed to religious contro versies, and who have no menus of gaining access to the books in which the answers to objections are to be found. You can scarcely

do a man a moro serious injury, than to destroy his peace of mind by unsettling his faith; most generally he will become first a doubter þÿ then a skeptick, nnd ultimately be left without the grace of Christ, without church ordinances, and " without God in the world." A very little observation and experience proves this. The example of referring to Dr. Moehler was set me by Professor Bush a Swedcnborgian in his reply to Dr. Woods, and we have ' the new and true paths," inconsistently following up his imputation upon me, with a quotation from a Mr. Ilayden containing a passage from a work of Mr. Newman published after ho had joined the Roman Catholic Church. If these are good authorities for, they must be equally good against Swedenborg " The new and true paths" makes this assertion "Dr. Moehler confesses that he had only read one solitary wotk of Swedenborg." This seems to be a stereotype calumny against every divine who presumes to expose the errors of Swedenborg. and 1 presume in nine cases out of ten it is a falsehood þÿ as it certainly is in the present instance. Dr. Moehler was treating of his theological system, and what he says is this, that Swedenborg's doctrines are set forth by him " The true nnd christian Religion dtc writing." " chiefly as they are staled in his last " [Symbolism p. 507 This work Swedenborg published just before his death as embodying his whole religious system nnd Dr. Moehler in his examination of that system, referred chief-

ly to it ; but be no where confesses as " the new and true paths" asserts, that he had only read that one work ; on the contrary he makes statements in the course of the nrticle, drawn from his other works, which he says was necessary, to complete his view of Swedenborg'8 system.

Swedenborg's assertion that we worship three Gods is altogether unfounded and untrue, we worship one God the Trinity in Unity. We have repeated the cavil on the passage in the Acts "only thev were baptised in the name of the Lord Jesus," which has been again and again answered. To do on act in the name of the King is to do it by his authority. To baptise in the name of the Lord Jesus, was to baptise by his authority, which he had just given them : " Go teach all nations baptising them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the lloly Ghost, &c." We are not for a moment to suppose the Apostles disobeyed this command of our Saviour, and that when administering Baptism, they used a form different from the one

he had proscribed. The reference to the Eulogium, pronounced before the house of nobles in Stockholm, by Mr Sondel, in proof of Swedenborg's theological erudition is peculiarly unfortunate, for while the Eulogy speaks in the highest praise

of his attainments in Mathematicks and various þÿsciences it speaks lightly, slightly and disparagingly of his theological writings, as the Swedenborgian editor is obliged to admit. In the earlier editions of the eulogy this part was suppressed by Swedenborg's disciples! A man may be well acquainted with triangles but this does not make him a learned theologian. It must be remembered that Swedenborg passed the first 50 years of his life engaged in secular learning and secular pursuits, and that at nearly tlitec score years, he entered upon his theological pursuits. L. p 1.) He claims to have been favoured during all this time with Oral instructions by the Deity and his Angels on the various subjects treated of in his theological writings. From the St. Thomas Times, July 31, 1850 The R. M. S. P. Go's. ship Df.r\>'ENT, arrived here yesterday from Southampton, site brought no mail, but some London papers to the 8th, which were kindly lent us by the company's superintendent. The news is extremely important to us, as we learn of a treaty of peace having been concluded between Denmark and Prussia, nothing however, beyond the outlines We are also extract below. given, which we learn of the demise of Sir Robert Peel and the probable abdication of the Emperor of Russia, for particulars of which see extracts.

Peace lias at length been concluded between Prussia and Denmark. The fact was officially announced yesterday in both Houses of Parliament. þÿ On the 1st instant at Berlin, at a Council of Ministers, at which the King was present, it was resolved to give a Prus- to the Danish ultimatum. The reply sian Government is prepared to enter into a treaty of peace, purely and simply reserving its respective rights, and incurring at the same time the obligation of lending its aid to the dissolution of the army of Schleswig llolstein; but on condition that an independent army shall be formed of the troops of llolstein, in order to allow the federal German army to quit the duchy. As to the internal affairs of Schleswig, the Prussian Government will leave their settlement to Denmark, the relations, however, hitherto existing between the Duchy and Denmark, not to be at present altered, the future relations of llolstein being reserved to the definitive settlement of the Central Power. The Prussian Cabinet will not, however, consent to the exclusive occupation of Rendsburgh and Fredericksort by the Danish troops, as such an occupation would imply the admission that those two places formed part of Schles-

Dcaili ol'Sir Robert Peel. Sir Robert Peel is no more. After þÿ three days of excessive suffering, the consequence of a fall from his horse on Saturday, at a few minutes past eleven on Tuesday night, the greatest statesman of his time quitted the scene in which lie had performed so conspicuous a part. Even the anxiety and the rumours which had penetrated every household since the first alarming intelligence failed to prepare " the country for the deplorable result. Except indeed, in the field of battle," as a writer in the Times has aptly remarked, never was " the transition from life to death so marked and so touching." On Friday, the House of Commons, which for more than forty years has witnessed the triumphs and reverses of the great Conservative chief, was filled with an extraordinary assemblage, anxious for the result of a great political crisis. Sir Robert, addressed them with an ability and a spirit which recalled his more youthful efforts, and more powerful days. It was the first occasion for four years that elicited any serious or direct opposition to the policy of her Majesty's tity. present advisers, and it is allowed that the speech was at least an admirable defence of the principles on which Sir Robert and his colleagues had ever proceeded. He sat down, as the report says, amid " loud and long-continued cheering." Within a few hours the statesman who had commanded the applause of that listening senate was a wreck of life and strength, shattered, feeble, restless, and agonised. The
feverish interval is past. That heart has ceased to beat; that tongue is ever still. That ardent spirit and capacious intellect are now in another and an unknown world.

During Saturday evening, Sir Robert was permitted to see Lady Peel and the members of his family; but after this time it was thought advisable to exclude all strangers from the apartment, for fear of producing any additional excitement. Sir Robert passed a restless night on Saturday, his extreme sensibility to touch increasing hourly, and his symptoms altogether becoming very alarming, which at the first, we believe, some of the medical gentlemen in attendance did not consider them to be. þÿ On Sunday evening, the pulse having increased from between SO and 00, at which it had ranged after the accident, to upw aids of 100, it was deemed necessary to take some blood, with a view of reducing (he inflammation. Twenty leeches were accordingly applied to the left shoulder by Dr. Foucart, and a large quantity of blood was obtained. There was no positive improvement in the condition of the patient from this operation, and he continued in a very precarious slate throughout the whole of Sunday and Monday. On Monda\ night, the alarming symptoms were greatly increased. About seven o'clock, Sir Robert became delirious, and attempted to raise himself up in bed. In this state he continued during the greater part of the night, and at intervals he became so much exhausted that his medical attendants were several times of opinion that he could not survive through O the night. o At two o'clock, far more dangerous symptoms than any which had yet been observed presented themselves. At this

time Sir Robert began to breathe stertorously and his senses again failed him. 11c ceased to answer any of the questions addressed to him, and appeared to be sinking into a comatose state. Sir Benjamin Brodie was again sent for, and on his arrival agreed with Dr. Foucart and the other medical gentlemen that the case now assumed a most dangerous aspect. The pulse had become very weak, and marked 118. From 2 o'clock to G o'clock, the change for the worse was progressive, the pulse increasing to Lit), and becoming gradually weaker. Stimulants were administered, but had no apparent effect, and the stertours breathing became more and more painful. The relatives were now informed that all the relief medical science could afford was exhausted and that no hope whatever existed of Sir Robert Peel's life being prolonged for twenty-four hours. The Bishop of Gibraltar (the Jlev. Dr. Tomlinson), a very old friend of Sir Robert's, was now sent for to administer the last offices of the Church. On the arrival of the prelate it was intimated to Lady Peel and the members of the family that they might, now, without risk of increasing the dangerous condition of the patient, be admitted to the apartment in which he was lying. In a few moments the whole family were assembled in the presence of their beloved relative, whose exhausted condition at this time scarcely enabled him to recognise their iden-

It is not the province of the journalist to violate the scantity of a scene like this, and therefore, this portion of our narrative necessarily omits all matters of detail. It is sufficient to say, that the lamented sufferer revived sufficiently during one period of the interview to identify the features of those þÿ ones surrounding his couch towards beloved whom he at length extended his faltering hand, in an attitude bespeaking the

intensity of his feelings, þÿ a voice scarcely audible "God bless whispered in you." Sir Robert ceased to exist at nine minutes before 11 o'clock. The earnest and spontaneous anxiety on the part of the population is, perhaps, the noblest eulogium that could be pronounced over his memory þÿ it was a touching and eloquent testimony that this man was dear to the hearts of the people, that his existence was considered by them a subject of national importance, and his popularity was as genuine as it was universal, that his name was cherished as much in the hovel as in the palace, by the poor as well as by the sovereign. Every circumstance connected with this manifestation of public sympathy will be lingered over with peculiar significance, and with no less satisfaction by the future historian þÿ who will recount how the Prince Consort in person hastened to the mansion of the departed statesman almost immediately after the occurrence of this most fatal accident, and how since that the purlieus of that classic neighborhood have been thronged with visitors, seeking eagerly tor the smallest scrap of intelligence that might give courage to their hopes, or in some measure alleviate their darker anticipations. Had the sufferer been a monarch, and that monarch one invested with an unusual prestige of popularity, more general sympathy could not by any possibility have been betrayed bv the population. The gates ofthe right lion, baronet's residence were literally besieged by the inquirers during the whole

of the Sunday, Monday and Tuesday, in so much that a strong body of constabulary was required to withstand pressure cit the persons assembled together; and these inquirers were actuated, moreover, not by idle curiosity as to the state of an individual ot large celebrity, but by solicitude for the safety of one who has gained the affections of the million. All the acrimony of partisanship, all the virulence ot political antagonism were merged in the gentleness of that all absorbing solicitude ; and it was u ith an emotion rather of pleasure than astonishment that the public observed among the multitude ot distinguished applicants for information the lion, gentleman the member for Buekinhamshire and the noble \iscount, Her .Majesty's principal Secretary for the Foreign Department. It was felt that such evidences of sympathy reflected honor at once upon the illustrious sufferer and upon those who thereby lowered the brands of political hostility before the awe inspired bv approaching dissolution.

RUSSIA. The news is important. Reports are in circulation, both at Berlin and Vienna, that the Emperor of Russia intends, on the 1st of December next, to abdicate in favor of his son, Alexander Nicholas. The motives of this resolution are stated to be þÿ A desire to retire from the fatigue of got eminent, and the recollection of the old superstition that no Russian Emperor can ever govern more than twentyfive years. A variety of particulars arc added, which would be interesting if the report were known to be true.

To the Editor of the St. Croix Avis. Sir, The article in your paper of Ihe 22nd July, hearing the signature of "E," is a very pretty little piece of composition. It reminds one somewhat ot his Schoolboy days, and of the very sublime themes, or specimens ot composition which we used to hand in on particular days of the the week, fessor, as case might be; and which, to the Master or Prowe were wont to flatter ourselves, contained a beauty of imagery, profundit y of thought, perfection of rhetoric, and accuracy of ratiocination that none could surpass, if, indeed, any could Professor's equal. But criticism alas! þÿ of our literary pro- The Master's or duction came in a day or two afterwards; and then the airy castle which our vanity alone had erected, came toppling down to the ground. 1 wish we could alibrd as much commendation for the subsequent part ol E's communication, which made its appearance iu your paper of the 25th July. Both parts exhibit a "plentiful lack" of argument; at least in so far as the doctrines of the New Church are concerned and this we deem the worst feature in them. The former part is written with some attention and care ; hut the latter is, in truth, neither move nor less than slovenly declamation, mixed up with scurrility; foul misrepresentations, and gross misquotations of" his opponents. " That agree We the columns of a Newspaper 18 with him in his remark the worst selected ground, whereon any subject connected with religion Ac., could possibly be discussed ;" and we

admit also the exception to ibis rule, that " there are occasions when we are called upon to give an account of the faith that is in us." Such an occasion presented itself when the recent attack of "The old paths" was made on the doctrines of the New Church. þÿ You may rest assured, Mr. Editor, that we should never have selected your, or any other public paper, in which to discuss disputed points on the subject of religion; but the task has been forced upon us. We are t lie less disposed to a contention of this sort, because among many reasons, we are of the class of different from laymen, whose that education lias been very which regular students of theology receive, who are properly educated for the Ministry in a Church; because we are unprovided with the hooks of reference which might better tit us for maintaining such a strife, and because we might be compelled to contend with clergymen who are supposed to be armed at all points, in such a contest, for lha purpose of defending by argument (not by denunciation merely) tbe particular tenets which tlicy advocate. We do not, however, say " Take any form but that ;" but we say, let our opponents present themselves in any form, even as clergymen, whether English Episcopalians or Roman Catholics, we fear them not. Our cause rests on the appeal which we can make to the reason of Mankind, and to I lie Word of the Old and New Testaments,

þÿ to the Word of God Himself ; and when the deductions made by our reason are confirmed, and amply confirmed too, by the very Word of God, who shall dare gainsay them '? þÿ As for the idle declamation and pithy denunciations of, more man, þÿ we value them not a ru8h.. þÿ Refute our doctrines by the Authority of the Holy Scriptures, þÿ and to these our reason shall succumb, but to mere human authority, the authority ot a Priesthood, not only in opposition to the obvious teaching of the Word oi God, but even to the plain inferences ot our reason, we will never submit. Your correspondent E., in the first part of his communication, has strung together a long list of truisms, as well as apparent truths, which have often been put to a similar use before ; and that too in somewhat of grandiloquent language, and ex-Cathedra style ; addresses them indiscriminately to the writer of the article in the Kiobenhavns Post (who is supposed to he a Danish clergyman), and to the members of the New Church, and then like Brutus in his speech over the dead body of Caesar, " pauses for a reply." The only fear him however, we answer we can give will not he quite so consolatory as that which the Roman received. In regard In the letter of the supposed Danish clergyman, we of the New Church do not feel ourselves hound in any way to offer a defence of it : we þÿ have nothing to do with it, except iu so far as we are required by Christian Charity to pity his blindness. We have been led, by that production, as well as

by a continuation of it which may he found in a subsequent number of ihe Kibheuhavns Post, to consider the writer of them to be in a very miserable state ; in a state very much resembling complete infidelity ; and we think it very probable that this infidel like state has been brought about by the perplexity of mind into which the writer has been cast l.y long continued, but fruitless efforts to reconcile the incomprehensible dogmas of the Old Churchmen and their perversion of truth, with the plain and obvious teachings of the Holy Scriptures. So far from deserving hlaiue for it, therefore, we humbly conceive that a truly christian spirit urged ou us the regret that no notice had been taken of that letter, more especially I y the followers of those individuals whom we conscientiously believe were tire real cause of the writer's perplexity and undecided faith. Something, however, lias been done to relieve him from his doubts, by a member of the New Church, and we sincerely pray and hope that his humble efforts to that effect, may be crowned with success. (To be concluded.)

IN order lo prevent the evils arising from an almost unrestricted trade with all sorts of commodities throughout the Island, carried on more especially by pedlars or travelling hucksters, it is hereby provisionally enacted and ordained as follows : I- Mercantile traffic is restricted to the towns of Christiansted and Frederiksted, and is not to be carried on out of the towns in the country. Labourers engaged on Estates, however, are permitted to sell by retail common articles of provision as well as candles, provided the sale takes place in their houses, on week-days and not during the working hours of the Estates. With regard to the sale of fish the provisional Regulation of the 2t)th January 1849 remains in force. 2. No person is permitted to trade in the towns either in his own name or in copartnership with others without a burghersbrief,

ATI So but exceptionally licences to carry on trade may be granted to females above 25 years of age. These licenses will be granted by the Governor General, on payment of $25, the Magistrate of Police having previously reported on the petition. The payment, however, may be reduced, on cause being shown. Widows of merchants and of petty dealers are entitled to continue the business of their late husband without any such licence. $ 3. All persons in the towns are permitted in his or her own dwelling house lo sell bread, candles, fruits, vegetables, cakes, sweetmeats, eggs, firewood and milk, and the Magistrate ol l'olice is hereby authorised to issue licences or passes for carrying the abovementioned uiticles about in the towns for sale, but the number of such licences shall not exceed 20 in Christiansted and 12 in Frederiksted. Such licence or pass is only to be granted lo individuals above 30 years of age, or to persons unable trom bodily infirmity to perform woik of a more laborious nature. These licences or passes shall he granted only for tire term of three months at a time, to be reckoned from the 1st of January, the 1st of April, the 1st of July and the 1st of October, but may be renewed, and are to be paid with $1 each tune. 4. With the exception mentioned in the above 3 all iratficing by itineiant sellers is hereby prohibited both in the towns and in the country. $ 5. All mercantile traffic mentioned in 2 shall bo subject to a tax Irom $2 to $10 quarterly to be paid before the expiration of

the fust month of the quarter. This tax shall be assessed by two persons for each town, of whom the Governor General appoints the one, and the llurgher Council the other. The assessment shall be made annually befote the 15th of January each year. Complaints of over-assessment shall be decided by the Governor General, the Burgher Council having previously repr i lea on the complaint. The petty trade mentioned in 3 is not liable to payment of taxes as above. 0. Masters of vessels and boats are permitted to sell their cargo on board their vessels or boals without paying any tax, but not to sell from stores or shops in the towns except on obtaining a burghersbrief, according to the direction m 2, and paying the tax, accoiding to 5. Masters of danish vessels however shall not be called on to take out a burghersbriel. Firewood, charcoal, fi mis, vegetables and olher ground provisions of the West India. Islands, turtles, fish and live stock may as hitherto be sold free of any tax, from the boats, on the wharves and landing bridges. 7. Those who have gained a livelihood hitherto by carrying on trade in the towns either from their own dwelling houses or by itinerant sellers without being in possession of a burghersbiief, shall also be entitled to carry on such trade in future in the towns and in their dwelling houses, provided they report themselves before the 1st October next to the þÿl olice Magistrate, who after having ascertained the correctness of their application will recommend them lo obtain a licence,

which will be granted by the Governor General free of expense. Such trade shall be liable to a tax from $1 to $5 quarterly according to the extent of the business, to be assessed in the manner directed in 5. 8. All fees and taxes imposed by this Regulation, are to be paid to the Land Treasurv, 9. The punishment of illegal trading is to be a fine of from $1 to 825, which fine is to be doubled in cases of repetition. The Goods thus disposed of shall be seized and caused to be sold by the Magistrate of þÿl olice, in the manner he may judge proper, for the payment of the fine. Persons not in the service of others carrying about goods for sale without a licence or pass are to be deemed vagrants and proceeded against accordingly. $ 10. This ordinance makes no alteration in the right of the country-labourers to sell on Saturdays in the towns vegetables, fruits, poultry and all other productions of their own industry. On other days they are only permitted to sell such articles in the towns when they ore provided with a pass from the manager of the Estate on which they ore domiciled. In default hereof the goods are to be seized and confiscated. The proprietors of estates art likewise as hitherto allowed to sell in the towns by their own servants meat, milk, fruits, vegetables, firewood and olher productions of their estates, yet if the sale takes place on other days than Saturdays, the seller must be provided with a pass from the proprietor, in default of which the goods will be seized and
confiscated.

$ II. It is the duty of the Magistrate of Police strictly to enforce the present Regulation. Transgressions of the same are to be proceeded against in the same manner as in public police cases. $ 12. This Regulation is to be enforced from the 1st of October next. The prohibitions and restrictions imposed by the general laws and the local regulations with regard to the sale of certain articles remain in force, therein included the existing regulations regarding the sale of rum and other spirituous liquors. IN order to prevent the evils arising from an almost unrestricted trade with all sorts of commodities throughout the Island, earned on more especially by pedlars or travelling hucksters, it is hereby provision, ally cuacted and ordained us follows: I. Mercantile tratlic is testiicied to the towns of Chrisiiansted and Frcderikstcd, and is not to be carried on out of the towns in the country. Labourers engaged on Estates, however, arc permitted to sell by retail common nrticles of provision as well as candles, provided the sale takes place in their houses, on week-days and not during the working hours of the Estates. With regard to the sale of fish the provisional Regulation of the 29llt Junuaiy 1849 remains in force. 2. No person is permitted to tiade in the towns cither in his own name or in copartnership with others w ithout a burghersbrief, but exceptionally licences to carry on trade may be granted to females above 25 j ears of age. These licences will be granted by the Governor General, on payment of $25, the Magistrate of þÿi oliee having previously reported on the petition. The payment, how. ever, may be reduced, on cause being shown. Widows of merchants and of petty dealers arc entitled to continue the business of their late husband without any such licence. $ 3. All persons in the towns arc permitted in his or her own dwelling house to sell bread, candles, fruits, vegetables, cakes, sweetmeats,

eggs, fuewood and milk, and the Magistrate of Police is hereby authorised to issue licences or passes for carrying the abovemention ed articles about in the towns for sale, but the number of such licences shall not exceed 20 in Christiansted and 12 in Frederiksted. Such licence or pass is only to be granted to individuals above 30 years of age, or to persons unable from bodily infirmity to perform work of a more laborious nature. These licences or passes shall be granted only for the term of three months at a tilne, to be reckoned from the 1st of January, the 1st of April, the 1st of July and the 1st of October, but may be renewed, and ate to be paid with $1 each time. 4. With the exception mentioned in the above 3 ail t latticing by itinerant sellers is hereby prohibited both in the towns and in the country. 5. All mercantile ti attic mentioned is: 2 shall be subject to a tax from $2 to $lti quarterly to be paid be foie the expiration of the (its! month of the quarter. This tax shall be assessed by two persons lor each town, of whom the Governor General appoints the one, and the Uurgher Council the other, 1 he assessment shall he made annua ly belote the 15th ol Junuaiy each year. Complaints of over- assessment shall be decided by the Governor General, the Dui þÿ gher Council having previously reported on the complaint. The petty trade mentioned in 3 is not liable to payment ol taxes as above. 6. Masters of vessels and boats are permitted to sell their cargo on board their vessels or

boats without paying any tax, but not to sell from stores or shops in the towns except on obtaining a burghersbrief, according to the direction in 2, and paying the tax, according to 5. Masters of danish vessels however slut I : not be c .lled on to take out a burghcisbnel. Firewood, charcoal, ft nils, vegetables and other ground provisions of the West India Islands, Duties, fish and livestock may as hitherto he sold lice of any tax, from the boats, on the wharves and landing bridges. $ 7. Those who have gained a livelihood hitherto by carrying on trade in the tow ns either from their own dwelling houses or bv itinerant selleis without being in possession of a burghersbrief, shall also be entitled to car rv on such trade in future in the towns and in their dwelling houses, provided they tepoit themselves before the 1st October next to the þÿl olice .Magistrate, who after having ascertained the correctness of their application will recommend them to obtain a licence, which will he granted by the Governor General free of expense. 8ueh trade shall he liable to a tax from $1 to $5 quarterly according to the extent of the business, to be assessed in the manner directed in 5. $ 8. All fees and taxes imposed by this Regulation, are to be paid to the Land Treasury 9. The punishment of illegal trading is to bo a fine of from $1 to $25, which fine is to be doubled in cases of repetition. The Goods thus disposed of shall bo seized and caused to be sold by the Magistrate of

police, in the munner he may judge proper, for t tie payment of the fine. Persons not in the service of others carrying about goods for sale without a licence or pass are to be deemed vagrants and proceeded against accordingly. 10. This ordinance makes no alteration in the right of the country-labourers to sell on Saturdays in the towns vegetables, fruits, poultry and all other productions of their own industry. On other days they arc only permitted to sell such articles in the towns when they are provided with a pass from the manager of the Estate on which they are domiciled. In default hereof the goods are to he seized and confiscated. The proprietors of estates are likewise as hitherto allowed to sell in the towns by their own servants meat, milk, fruits, vegetables, firewood arid other productiors of their estates, yet if the sale takes place on other days than Saturdays, the seller must he provided with a pass from the proprietor, in default of which the goods will be seized and confiscated. Jilt is the duty of the Magistrate of Police sti icily to enforce the present Regulation. Transgressions of the same are to be proceeded against in the same manner as in public police eases. 12. ST. MOII AVIS. Cliristianslcd, 22d August 1850. The news brought us by the la«t packet, which arrived here yesterday morning, is very interesting and satisfactory. The gallant danish troops, under coinknaml of General Krogh, struck a severe blow at the Insurgents, at Idstedt, on the 25th of July last. The Danes lost 12 dead and 73 wounded officers, 104 dead and 2.300 wounded non-commissioned officers and privates. The loss of the Insurgents is very great þÿ upwards of 2,000 were in the Slesvig hospitals þÿ 1,000 were taken prisoners, and a great number killed. þÿ The intelligence was gladly received here þÿ the inhabitants were in ecstacy þÿ the fort tired a royal salute, in honor of the event þÿ and, in the evening, illuminations were general, in consequence of so glorious an achievement of Valor and Victory !

In conformity to tlic arrangements made, the 2nd brigade of the 2nd Division of the Army advanced from Havetoft at 14 þÿo clock on the morning of the 25th July, and the 5th Brigade marched from Helligbtek at 4 þÿo clock. This Brigade first came into collision with the enemy and commenced the battle which soon extended very considerably on the right wing, which the enemy endeavoured to out-flank. Several Battalions of the 1st Division were sent against the enemy and drove them back. The weather was very unfavorable, heavy rain and fog þÿ so that nothing could be seen rt nnv great distance. IVo filing was heard castwardly and nothing was heard from the 2nd Division. Under these circumstances, as information was obliged to he procured by sending out Officers and orderlies, the 5th Brigade was commanded not to advance farther hut sta-

tionary to maintain the contest, for which support was sent them from the reserve of artillery. Bulow wounded, all of whom were among the most gifted officers of the army. so sudden not he otherwise than that It could a loss among the superior officers and their staff should create a pause, and occasion some confusion in the mameuvres. This, however, was speedily remedied. General von Meza was sent to the spot with an organised þÿstall to , com-

s or. a a t 'i 3. mand the 2nd Division.. The General went thither at 8 þÿo clock ; three Battalions of the 4th Brigade under Colonel v. Thestrup had, however been earlier sent off to join the forces there under Colonel v. Baggesen. Meanwhile as these Battalions of the right flank which previously had been pushed in advance had not as yet returned, it was resolved that the forcing of the. passes should be delayed one hour, at the expiration of which the whole line should energetically move onward. The 3rd Brigade had, however, advanced against Sollbro, þÿ though first after an engagement þÿ and after having thrown a bridge across the stream under the fire of the enemy, had forced the passage. The enemy, subsequently, was briskly driven hack upon Jiibek ; afterwards the Brigade by the way of Silberstedt at 11 4 þÿo clock, arrived before Schuby, which was fired upon. At 104 þÿo clock the main body of the army marched forward to storm and force j that with itself through the fortified pass between Arnholzsoe and Langsb. Alter a severe con1est«of Artillery this was accomplish- I ed by the Battalions of the 4th and (Jtli Brigades, among which the Foot-Guards, under Colonel v. Irmingcr were sent forward, in conjunction with the Brigade of Colonel v. Haulers, to force the passes on the left side of the small lake situated between the two Lakes previously mentioned, whilst part of the 4th Brigade was to form a Corps of Reserve at this point, and whilst Major General von Meza with the remainder

of the 2nd Brigade, and a little more than 3 Battalions of the 4th Brigade, as a reserve, placed themselves on the Eastern side of the small Lake aforesaid. The obstinate resistance which hitherto had taken place against the passing through the wood in front of j these passes was broken by this attack j þÿ a res stance that was heigthened hv I the impassable nature of the ground on both sides of the road, which made them long defiles For the reserve cavalry, that was drawn up with the main body, there was as yet no kind of employment. þÿ The Jst Brigade had, meanwhile been detached against Wedelspang, not however to force this pass ; it had two Battalions in Ovre-llolk and the rest thereof in the direction of Wedelspang. The prohematicul attempt of the 3rd Brigade was thus completely accomplished by Colonel v. Schepelern, and whose arrival at Schuby by corresponding so exactly with the advanced movement of the main body through the passes, contributed not a little to the speedy abandonment of the entrenchments by the enemy. The orders which under earlier unfavorable circumstances were thus sent to the Brigade, and which in consequence of the difficult communication could only he forwarded by crossing an almost impassable territory, had meanwhile hindered the movements of the Brigade being pursued in an easterly direction, occasioned less profitable results, than otherwise might have occurred. At the junction of the Chalsee and the old road, and the adjoining

heights on the way to St. Jurgen, the main body now advanced rapidly ; here the reserve cavalry were detached against Lyrskov and Schuby, to clear those places, which was effected by aid of the Battery þÿ þÿWegener. The 4th and Gth Brigades, on the other hand were directed against Schuby, whilst the rest of the main body took up a position on Ihe heights north of Slesvig. After having searched the wood west of Slesvig it advanced about 8 þÿo clock through this town to bivouac on the road from

Haddeby - Noor, behind Dannevirkc, leading to Schuby. The 3rd Brigade bivouacked nigh Neukrug as a reserve. This position was taken about midnight, and Headquarters was then first established at Slesvig which was garrisoned by a Battalion. The enemy is supposed to have retreated with his main body to Rcndsborg, and with one Brigade to Eckernforde. His loss has been very great. Upwards of 1,000 prisoners are taken. Two guns of þÿBaggesen s Battery which had been captured at the assault at Ovre-llolk, arc retaken, independent of 5 pieces of artillery captured from the enemy. In the Slesvig hospitals are found about 2,000 wounded insurgents. Besides which the majority of those w ho lay in ambush at Ovrellolk arc killed, and the greater part of the town burnt. Mai.y dead bodies of the enemy lie still unburied in the fields, as not a solitary waggon could he found here. Our victory has strengthened the moral element among the soldiers, so unrepining endurance they have borne the privations, and matchless exertions they latterly have been subjected to. The most excellent discipline lias been maintained, and no excesses have come to the knowledge of the Uoiumandcr-in-Cliicf. 41c, how ever, lament the loss of many and dear sacrifces. The i nihiish cost us several of our most distinguised officers, and w e have in all, no less than 12 dead and 73 wounded officers, 104 dead, and 2,300 wounded non-commissioned oilieers and privates. The Army is nevertheless in high condition. These are ihe essential out-
lines of a battle between two armies, w ho by nature and the development of circumstances are destined to act in j unison. By command, (signed) Christian Gap.

I hereby call the attention of the whole body of Planters in this Island to the great inconvenience experienced by the Planter, in moulding the canes with the plough, from the trash, which must, under our present system, be removed by manual labor preceding the plough. The society convinced of the loss of labor occasioned thereby, have resolved to offer a premium of the value of One Hundred Dollars, to any individual who will invent, for the benefit of Planters at large, an implement, attached to the front of the plough, by which the trash may lie turned over at the same time that the plough mould the cane. If tonnage-dues are paid at one of the Customhouses of this Island, or at St. Thomas, additional tonnage-dues are ir» he paid, only in case the vessel should again discharge or load during the same voyage, goods to such an amount, that, together with the previous amount discharged or loaded, it shall reach a quantity, on which a higher tonnage-due is fixed. At Christiansted, vessels arc further to pay one half the amount of tonnage dues, at the above rate, for keeping the harbour with wharves and other appurtenances in repairs.
