Your correspondent E, adopting the usual course of others, his predecessors, who have attacked, not with argument, hut with calumny and misrepresentation, the theological doctrines taught hy Swedenborg, deliberately confounds the questionings of the writer in the Kjdbenhavns Post with the teachings of the new Church, and propounds his truisms, and applies his notions and remarks to both without distinction, and thereby basely and falsely endeavours to lead the reader to the erroneous conclusion that said questionings and teachings emanate from one and the same source. One thing, however, E. has not yet done, he has not shown that he knows what the doctrines ol the new Church are : on the contrary, lie betrays the grossest ignorance of them. We had it to be an undeniable rule or law of always supposed criticism þÿ that the critic should know what he was þÿcriticising, but it would appear from the example set ns by E. that a polemic in the theological doctrines may dispense with that rule. yet he adopts these as his own by approving of them, and by requesting you to insert them in your paper. He also, is led to his unwarranted attack on the New Church by the letter extracted from the Kidbcnhavns Post; and in doing so evinces, equally as much as E., his ignorance as to what the doctrines of that Church really teach. How they reconcile such conduct with their consciences, is to us quite incomprehensible ; but they delight in incomprehensibles ; and perhaps will tell us that their conduct is not only admissible, but also quite correct, that according to the maxim of the Jesuits, þÿ the end sanctifies the þÿmeans; and the High Church lians resemble, in not a few Episcopa- party, the Puseyites, of the respects, the Jesuits; nay, we believe that they have, by some, been occasionally deemed Romanists in disguise ; so that, in one way or another, whether they be Romanists or Episcopalians, they are sure, by some sort of jugglery, to crawl out of the dilemna. We, on the contrary, who hold to þÿ the law and the þÿtestimony only, have always believed that the same God who forbad us to steal, to murder, to commit adultery, likewise forbids us to bear false witness against our neighbours, and we have been accustomed to deem all his commands as equally stringent. Your correspondent E., in the beginning of his letter evidently wishes to insinuate (but in rather ambiguous phrase, in order that he may he able, we suppose to creep away from the charge of bearing false witness) that

the letter of the supposed Danish cler- þÿ gyman, and that signed The new and true þÿpaths, are alike intended as a defence of the doctrines taught by Swedenborg ; but we are totally at a loss to imagine how the former of these letters could be deemed a defence of these dootrinestffor it appears to carry on the face of it something very like a denial of the Trinity ; whereas Swedenborg most urgently enforces the doctrine of a Trinity as taught in the Word of God,

Regard also the wonders wrought in our own day by Steam, and remember also how impossible they were before deemed. Should we not say that they were ignorant of the law of progression to which man is subject? And if the Trinity has been, as all Theologians agree, a subject of considerable doubt and uncertainty, should we therefore suppose that the God of Wisdom would everlastingly suffer these things remain so ? þÿ The Lord himself declares that there would be a time when lie would clearly reveal þÿhimself, These things have I spoken unto you in proverbs, (or, as it is given in the margin, 1 shall in parables) no more speak unto you in pro- but the time cometh when verbs, (or parables) but shall show you plainly of the Father þÿ John 16,25. To Christians in general, has that time ever come yet ? Whatever clearness of perception the apostles themselves might receive respecting it after the day of Pentecost, certainly, such plainness has never yet been general in the Church. Disputes respecting the person of our Lord, and his relation to the Father, arose in the very first ages ; and the decisions ot the Council of Nice, and the Athanasian Creed, tended still more to involve the subject in abscurity. Does the Christian church, as existing generally at the present day, possess the

promised plain knowledge þÿof the Father? is it to be found in the doctrina of the Trinity, as commonly maintained? Alas! what pretensions to plainness can be claimed for a doctrine, whose advocates prepare the minds of their disciples for receiving it, by telling them that they must never hope to understand it, that it is, in truth, utterly incomprehensible. Surely, with the promise in our bibles, that the doctrine of the Trinity and of the relation of the person of the Lord Jesus Christ to the Father should be made plain, and with the knowledge which we all have that in the doctrines of all Christian churches at present existing, it is avowedly any thing but plain, we ought at any rate to look with candour upon any new view which professes to clear the doctrine from its obscurity, and which boldly claims, and not without good grounds, when fairly examined, to make the subject at least consistent, and to combine in its favor all the suffrages of reason and all the testimony of the þÿScriptures. This intelligence will be received here and throughout Europe with extreme satisfaction, and the pleasure with w hich we hail the conclusion of peace now is only abated by our surprise that it w as not concluded on the same terms many months ago, since the combined remonstrances of England, France, and Russia, on this question must at any lime have produced the same result. Prussia had argued in the later stages of the negotiation that though she had 4>cen ready, and was empowered, to make

war on behalf of the Germanic Confederation. yet that her powers derived from that august but impalpable body did not extend to the conclusion of peace, and that as no legal representative of the Federal authority existed, so, in fact, no legal and binding peace with Germany could be concluded Denmat k very naturally declined to accede to the subtlety of this distinction, and positively required that whenever she sheathed the sword and laid up Iter men of war, she should at least have the assurance that her rights were acknowledged by all the world, and that the peace were complete. To this demand the King of þÿI ni ssiA has at last submitted, and he has withdrawn ftont the contest for himself and for the Bund; the justice of the case, as far as he is concerned, is satisfied, in spite of the absurdity of his act in one important transaction on behalf of a hody whose authority and existence he has denied elsewhere. It would be an endless and ungracious task to collect the contradictious and inconsistencies into which Lrussia has b':en led by her luckless and discreditable

3 © 31 © 2 21 ATI 3 connivance with the insurrection of the Duchies and the Danish war. 'I he peace now concluded at Berlin, appears to be an unconditional abandonment ol every prin ciple for which Germany had professed to caie and to contend. The Duchies will he divided; no conditions are innoducod with reference to the separate administration of Schleswig ; and the Stadtholdeiute, entirely forsaken by itsclamoious allies, is left either

to make terms with its Sovereign or to light it out with Denmark. We may veniuie, therefore, to claim for the views which we have defended the merit of a more sincere re gard for the true interests and honor of Germany than has been evinced by her own champions ; and we sincerely hope that when next her armies take the field it w ill not he for the destruction of a feeble and friendly State in the teeth of public opinion, throughout Europe, but in some cause identified w ith the rights and liberties of Germany and ol those great objects which the awakened spirit of the German nation will not cease to pursue But if these comments are suggested by the abortive enterprise and the crooked policy of the German States in this war, wo must hasten to add that every part of these trying events has thrown additional lustre on the spirit, the ability, and the courage of Denmark, in her Sovereign, her states-men, and her people. That form of government is always popular, that nation is always united, that State is always secure, in which all ranks take their stand with confidence arid energy upun their public rights, arid contend as one man in delence of them. The just renown which Denmark has earned by her constancy and her courage in a struggle against the whole Confederation of Germany bears no proportion to her own diminutive territories. Her cause was sound ; on one element she enjoyed a superiority of which all the armies of Germany could not deprive her and though she has had less of the diieci

support of other Lowers, than was due to her, she has the more entirely maintained her own independence of action and she has the more deserved tiie respect and sympathy of Europe. If the natives of Schleswig- Holstein had their choice of belonging to one political body or to the other þÿ the Danish Monarchy or the German Confederation þÿ Printed and and if that choice were to be determined by the spirit shown in this contest, they ought to

esteem it an honour to resume their place i the ranks of the Danish arn y and the scuts of the Danish Legislature and their mercantile, maritime, and political interests all point, not to separation, hut to the closest union. The leaders of the insurrection in the Duchies must now see that their mischievous enterprise is at an end, for as they have failed to obtain the active support of Germany and failed to prevent the conclusion of this peace, it would merely cause a useless effusion of blood, to he followed necessaiilv bv their own ruin, if they were now so foolhardy as to renew the war. No success which they woo'd obtain against the Grown of Denmark, even if the Holstein army were allowed to cross the Eider, could improve their position or alier a resolution approved by a!! the great Lowers of Europe. They may now lay down their arms with comparative honour, but if the war be unhappily renewed, their defeat would be destructive, and their advance would only increase the danger of a foreign occupation. It is the height of absurdity to represent this contest as a struggle for the principles of freedom or for national independence. The terms on which the Duchies may now live under the Danish Crown are far more literal tin n those which Denmark had herself enjoyed for the proceeding 150 years, when she was not, as she now is, a constitutional State; and this stiife between kinsmen and neighbours within a small territory is a civil war between two countries whose national inter-

ests and obligations are the same. The Duchies will not be absorbed or extinguished by Denmark any more than Wales or Scotland have been annihilated by England ; the western principality nnd ihe northern kingdom have retained all their characteristic traditions of race and usages, and of law, but they have received in addition an ample share of the power and prospeiitv of the United Kingdom. The greatest nations of the world have owned and have cherished some such divided origin, and of all the popular illusion let loose upon the world by the storm of 1848, the most dangerous and extravagant was that Slate and Empiie were to tie decomposed and dissolved into their primitive national elements. The attempt was actually made at a great saciifne of ihe public peace, for it threatened to annihilate several States, of which Denmark was one, and to alter the territorial arrangements of all Europe; hut we tiust that experiment is the last of the kind, and we venture to assert. not as a paradox, but as a political truth confirmed by experience, that nothing is more conducive to the stability, the strength, and the welfare of States than the fusion and union of different races, of provincial institutions, and of several various forms of natioi al growth and culture, not at all reduced to one standard, but conducing in their several wavs to form the character and to direct the activity of a þÿnation.

The way in which the truth upon this subject became distorted, appears manifest from Ecclesiastical history. It was more especially in the early part of the fourth century, that the Divine Trinity became a subject of controversy in the Church. To the decision of the celebrated Council of Nice in Biihynia, convoked in the year 325, may he tiaced the origin of the lripersonality of God, which with various modifications and modes of explanation, has existed ever since jn the Uld Chuich, as its fundamental and leading doctrine. In this Nicene Council, the doctrine of Arius, on whose accouui it was convoked, was formally condemned; a doctrine which taught that the Bon of God was a created being, totally and essentially distinct from, and inferior to, the Father, both in naiurc, person, and dignity. The Council, in opposition to this doctrine, declared tlrut the l ather, Son and Holy Spirit were three þÿ hypostases " that they were þÿ homoousioi'' i. e. ot the same naluie, dignity and essence, equal and consubstantial : and from the words in which the decision of that Council is expressed, there is no reason for supposing that they entertained any tiling like the commonly received idea of three persons in the Tiinily þÿ a doctiine that was subsequently evolved or extorted from them; for the Greek woid hypostasis, properly signifies the basis, substance, or ground of

being, that which is essential lo the existence of any thing. The iauguage of the Nicene Council, theiefore, properly translated, would convey this idea, that in the Divine Nature or Being tiiere are three essentials, expressed by the terms Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, without which the Divine Being could not have existence ; and this is the real truth þÿ Subsequently the word hypostasis was translated into the Latin persona, which at that time signified a mask, an appearance, or an assumed character ; whence the origin of dramatis persona, now in use in dramatic writings. But when, at a later period the word persona came to be applied to the real individual þÿ man or woman þÿ and hence was afterwards translated into the English word person ; we see, that the signification of the original word hypostasis was entirely lost. Thus, through gradual change a in the conventional use and meaning of a term þÿ a change incident to the mutability of human language, and facilitated in no small degree by successive translations þÿ we may discover how the statement of a doctrine, which, according to the meaning of the terms, in which it was originally expressed, may have been true, came at length lo involve and teach a falsity. To say as the writer þÿ E does, that we attach great importance to the fact that Swedenborg wrote thirty volumes on theological subjects, is, we are sorry to say a misrepresentation of our words ; for we merely observed that although Swedenborg had written thirty

volumes on this subject, Dr. Moehler confesses that he had road but one of his works, now published in a single volume octavo. þÿ In an age like þÿthis, says E, þÿ we are very naturally inclined to judge of a þÿman m s erit, not so much

by the quantity as by the quality of what he writes, þÿ Would E have us to believe that lie has judged Swedenborg by the quality of what he wrote 1 I dare venture to assert that þÿ þÿE has not read one single line of what Swedenborg has written, except what he was forced to read in our communication. I should sooner think that he has neither judged of these writings by their quality, or brought them, as he says, þÿ to the tribunal of Gods holy Word but that he has judged them according to idle rumours, according to their agreement or disagreement with the tenets of his Church, (which every one, we are sure, has by this time perceived to be the Romish Church ;) his judgement, therefore, cannot but be unfavorable. But in tliis we glory, for we would indeed be sorry if they did agree with those tenets. As regards the assertion of þÿSwedenborg h s aving þÿ diseased a þÿbrain, we deny this, and call for the proof. W e, who have perused þÿSwedenborg s works find every tiling orderly, scriptural, and consistent ; and as for dreams and visionary legends, we beg to refer the writer and reader to þÿ þÿButler sLives of the þÿSaints, as being replete with such. As to þÿ casting Swedenborg and his books to the four winds of þÿheaven, we imagine this to be a difficult task for the Church of Rome to accomplish just now, for the former being dead long since, she would have to content herself with casting his ashes to the winds, as she did those of Wycliffe, whose remains, forty years after his death, were taken up and burned,

and his ashes scattered on the river Swift by order of the then reigning Pope. And with regard to the latter (his writings,) she would, in order to destroy them, be obliged to expend a large amount, and then she will but furnish additional means to the publishers to issue New Editions; for they, fortunately, now abound in Protestant countries. As for the manner in which þÿ þÿE his caricatured the words of Mr. Noble, we will but remark, that it only requires, that any one should read that passage again, as contained in our first communication, in order to perceive that it was an explanation adopted by Mr. Noble in order that perverted minds may be able to understand how þÿ the Three that bear record in heaven are þÿOne, and in no manner does Mr. Noble say that these terms arc to be substituted in the Bible for those Holy Names wiiich are here applied þÿ to the only Wise God our Saviour (Jude 25 verse.) We have been enabled to ascertain the accuracy of the remark that Chrysostom flourished chiefly in the fourtli century, the error is due to the treachery of our memory ; but still we maintain that the conclusion we drew from his prayer inserted in the book of Common Prayer, holds good, and is perfectly correct. Not the slightest allusion is therein made to any thing like Tripcrsonalism, neither can we perceive that the quotation, given by E, from his sermon, indicates a belief in three persons, although it may have reference to three Essentials. It is, however, of very little con-

sequence what this Archbishop of Constantinople, or any other of the bishops of the same period taught ; for their opinions were generally sucli as tallied with þÿ their own interests, or the interests of their party ; we have the scriptures for our guide in forming correct ideas of God, and also of the Trinity, in unity. þÿ From sucli accounts as we have of Chrysostom, we are disposed to allow that lie, more steadily than most others of the clergy of his time, pursued what he deemed the path of integrity. It is, therefore, somewhat remarkable that he who wrote in the same century as that in which the Nicene Council was held, should have omitted to make especial mention of the supposed three persons of the Godhead in one of his prayers which seems intended for repetition at each meeting for public worship. Should E. be disposed to favor us with any more of his observations on doctrines of Theology, we trust that lie will bring the proof of his assertions from the Word of God, and not from any doubtful or human source. If doctrines be true, there ought and can be found sufficient, nay abundant proofs of their truth, in the Scriptures of the Old and New Testament. This we assert of the doctrines of the New Church ; and we arc willing to defend them on this, the best ground. The new and (rue paths.

amtaKKMQga California. We have dates from San Francisco to May 1. The gold-digging is represented as in a highly prosperous condition. The new settlement at Trinidad Bay promises to he a place of a good deal of importance. On a beautiful plateau on the northern shore of the bay, the site of a town has been surveyed, and buildings are now erecting in considerable numbers. The harbour is said to be the finest on the coast, with the exception of San Francisco and San Diego. The Legislature had adjourned, after a session of 100 days, having passed 143 acts, most of which were essential to the complete organisation of the State Government. The people expressed a decided adherence to the position they have assumed m favor of free soil and a free constitution. Illustrated London News, June 29. The News from California.þÿ The news from this golden region of the þÿl acilic is interesting, but not astonishing. Commerce and civilization seem to he settling down upon the same principles of action to which we are accustomed for many years past, in these regions of the l nion. Prices are much moderating in ail the great staples in þÿ land, timber, food and folly. There seems to be no end to the discoveries of new gold places ; and the prospects of tiie coming summer are as brilliant as ever they were before. Emigration is still increasing, piety is spreading, churches are building, gambling houses and hells are patronized to any reasonable extent, politics are organizing on the old platforms, and everything is

going on swimmingly. The political movements are not without their significance. The Legislature has been in session for a few month j past; but we do not hear of the propositions formerly started m that body, to take the Custom House into their own hands and begin a movement looking towards a separation from the old Atlantic States. In the Senate, however, Mr. Douglass submitted a concurrent resolution, which was adopted, providing for the appointment of a committee on the part of each house, to take into consideration the subject of the immediate admission of California into the Union. According to the tone of the journals, and other organs of public opinion, they seem to look upon any movements towards dis-

ST, 0 3i -t> I 2 AT2 3» union of any kind, with as much opposition and horror as we do here in the United States. There is no danger of California flying þÿoil at the handle, for the present. The evils of a revolution and change of trade seem to have exhausted themselves, and things, we are happy to say, seem to be gradually coming to their proper bearings again, and success settling over all California. Gold is as plenty as ever.

Singular Prophecy. Lorenzo Dow, of eccentric memory, was in possession of a German work on the Prophecies, which he valued highly, and frequently made quotations from. Among other remarkable sayings of the author, were these : þÿ þÿ I would not be a king, in þÿ1843. I would not be a grave digger, in þÿ1849. þÿ I would not be a soldier, in þÿ1850. þÿ I would be either, in þÿ1851. The work alluded to was written about 200 years ago. It certainly possesses an interest for the curious. How frail the tenure by which kings held their crowns, in 1843 ! Who would like the office of grave digger in 1849, unless he was solely mercenary ? How more than presumable is it that the earth will contribute multitudes, in 1350, to till a wide and quiet grave ! And we may hope, at least, in 1851, for the fair harbingers which promise þÿ peace on earth, and good will to þÿmen. Journal of Commerce.

Good Advice. John 11. Prentice, in Ins recent valedictory on retiring from the editorial chair, which he has tilled for forty-two years, has the following : þÿ þÿ No man should be without a wellconducted newspaper, lie is far behind the spirit of the age unless he reads one, is not upon ail equal footing with his fellow-mail who enjoys such advantage, and is disregardful of his duty to his liimily, in not affording them an opportunity of acquiring a knowledge of what is passing in the world, at the cheapest possible teaching. Show me the family without a newspaper, and I venture to say that there will be manifest in that family a want of amenity of manners, and indications of ignorance most strikingly in contrast with the neighbor who allows himself such a rational indulgence. þÿ Young men, especially, should read newspapers. If I were a boy, even of twelve years, I would read a newspaper weekly, though I had to work by torchlight to earn money enough to pay for it. The boy who reads will learn to think and analyse ; and, if so, he will be almost sure to make a man of himself, hating vicious indulgence, which reading is calculated to beget a distaste þÿfor.

A Man of Wealth A man of wealth, living a stranger to religion and its ordinances, was walking and holding this soliloquy þÿ þÿ What a happy man 1 am ! I have an ample fortune, an affectionate wife, and every thing to make me comfortable ; and what is more, 1 am indebted to no one for it, 1 have made it myself; I am independent of every one; it is all my own. Many persons are under obligations, here and

there, but I am not. It is all my own." At that instant a sudden shower of rain drove him to the nearest church. He went in, and just at that moment the minister rose and read his þÿtext þÿ Ye are not your own, ye are bought with a þÿprice. þÿ this is a strange doctrine. But it does þÿ What! (said he to himself) not apply to me ; I am my own, and all that 1 have is my þÿown. The course of the sermon exposed his obligations to God, and issued, in totally revolutionizing his views and feelings.

þÿAlligator Aesf. s They resemble, says Lyell, in his second visit to America, haycocks about four feet high and five in diameter at their bases, being constructed with grass and herbage. First they deposit one layer of eggs on a floor of mortar, and, having covered this with a second of mud and herbage, eight inches thick, lay another set of eggs upon that, and so on to the top ; there being commonly from one to two hundred eggs in a nest. With their tails they then beat down round the nest the dense grass and reeds five feet high, 'to prevent the approach of unseen enemies. The female watches her eggs until they are hatched by the heat of the sun, and then takes her brood under her care, defending them and providing for their subsistence; Dr. Luzenberger, of New Orleans, told me that he once packed up one of these nests, with the eggs, in a box for the museum of St. Petersburgli, but was recommended before he closed it to see that there was no danger of any of the eggs being hatched on the voyage. On opening one, a young alligator walked out, and was soon follow ed by the rest, about a hundred, which he fed in his house, when they went up and down the stairs whining and barking like young puppies. They ate voraciously, yet their growth was so slow as to confirm him in the opinion that alligators which have attained the largest size are of very great age ; though whether thev live tor three centuries, as some pretend, must be decided by future observation.

Midnight Harmonic. It is said of the saintly George Herbert, the quaint old English Church poet, that once, in a walk to Salisbury, to join a musical party, he saw a poor man with a poorer horse, that was fallen under his load. They were both in distress, and needed present help, which Mr. Herbert perceiving, putoffhis canonical coat, and helped the poor man to unload, and afterwards to load his horse. But a short time elap- headway, with the llumes spreading in to ;lb families sed before that large building, through to Water street, was enveloped in ll.anes; and the one adjoining on the North, No. 80, was on lire, as well as the one south, No. 70. Several persons were knocked down, as if dead, and hundreds ran over them, causing legs and arms to be broken, and injuries inflicted of a very serious character. In the flight, some were thrown into the Delaware, while a large number jumped voluntarily into the river, to shield themselves from the bricks and cinders thrown from the burning stores.
